Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and why does knowledge distillation outperform learning from raw data? The paper investigates this by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to interpret knowledge distillation by quantifying visual concepts encoded in intermediate layers of DNNs, and proposes and verifies three hypotheses explaining why knowledge distillation leads to better performance than learning from raw data.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation ensures DNNs learn more task-relevant concepts, have a higher learning speed (simultaneous concept learning), and optimize with less detours than learning from raw data, as verified by the proposed quantification metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more task-relevant visual concepts and fewer task-irrelevant concepts than learning from raw data.
Knowledge distillation ensures the DNN learns various visual concepts simultaneously, whereas learning from raw data tends to learn concepts sequentially.
Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions (fewer 'detours') than learning from raw data.
The proposed entropy-based metrics can quantify and compare visual concepts across different layers and network architectures.
Experiments on multiple DNN architectures and datasets generally support the three hypotheses.
papers.limitation:
The work only focuses on the classification task; applying the methods to other tasks (e.g., object segmentation) or data types (e.g., video) is theoretically feasible but not explored.
The learning procedure of DNNs cannot be precisely divided into a learning phase and a discarding phase; the target epoch for measuring concept richness is a rough estimation.
future_direction: Applying the proposed methods to other tasks such as object segmentation.
Applying the proposed methods to other types of data such as video.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the hidden states in models of different scales? The paper investigates whether there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models trained on similar data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Linear Representation Transferability (LRT) Hypothesis and provides empirical evidence that affine mappings between hidden states of different-sized models can transfer steering vectors, enabling small models to steer large models.
papers.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence for the LRT hypothesis, suggesting that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the hypothesis is a promising direction for understanding representation alignment across model scales.
papers.key_findings:
Affine mappings can be learned between the hidden states of small and large models from the same family.
Steering vectors learned on small models retain their semantic effect when transferred to large models via the learned affine map.
The transferred steering vectors are as effective as those learned directly on the large model for tasks like refusal behavior removal and logit-based evaluation.
The feature spaces of models, as represented by sparse autoencoder decoder matrices, are approximately linearly related.
The conceptual framework of a universal representation space provides a plausible explanation for the linear transferability.
papers.limitation:
The limits of transferability across very different model sizes (e.g., 100M to 70B) are not yet understood.
Transferability across different model families or architectures is challenging due to differences in tokenization schemes and architectural design.
future_direction: Investigating the limits of transferability across model sizes.
Exploring transferability across different model families and architectures.
Developing theoretical foundations for the LRT hypothesis and the universal representation space.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that neural networks with similar architectures trained on similar data learn shared representations relevant to the learning task. We build on this idea by extending the conceptual framework where representations learned across models trained on the same data can be expressed as linear combinations of a \emph{universal} set of basis features. These basis features underlie the learning task itself and remain consistent across models, regardless of scale. From this framework, we propose the \textbf{Linear Representation Transferability (LRT)} Hypothesis -- that there exists an affine transformation between the representation spaces of different models. To test this hypothesis, we learn affine mappings between the hidden states of models of different sizes and evaluate whether steering vectors -- directions in hidden state space associated with specific model behaviors -- retain their semantic effect when transferred from small to large language models using the learned mappings. We find strong empirical evidence that such affine mappings can preserve steering behaviors. These findings suggest that representations learned by small models can be used to guide the behavior of large models, and that the LRT hypothesis may be a promising direction on understanding representation alignment across model scales.

papers.title: Knowledge is a Region in Weight Space for Fine-tuned Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the relationships between different finetuned language models in weight space, and how do these relationships affect model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned language models form well-defined regions in weight space where interpolation yields high performance, and starting from the centroid of these regions improves efficient finetuning.
papers.conclusion: There are regions in weight space corresponding to good performance on datasets or tasks, and models within these regions share capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned models on the same dataset cluster tightly in weight space.
Linear interpolation between finetuned models produces models with comparable or better performance.
The convex hull between models defines a region of low loss, indicating shared knowledge.
Extrapolation beyond the region quickly degrades performance.
Averaging models to get the centroid of a region provides a better starting point for efficient finetuning than the pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on finetuning a pretrained model, not random initialization.
Focused on English classification data.
Mixed results for domain groups like Twitter.
Did not replicate on many pretrained models.
future_direction: Understanding how iterative averaging processes move through weight space.
Exploring the limitations of gradient-based training in reaching optimal points within regions.
papers.abstract: Research on neural networks has focused on understanding a single model trained on a single dataset. However, relatively little is known about the relationships between different models, particularly those trained or tested on different datasets. We address this by studying how the weight space and the underlying loss landscape of different models are interconnected. Specifically, we demonstrate that finetuned models that were optimized for high performance, reside in well-defined regions in weight space, and vice versa -- that any model that resides anywhere in those regions also exhibits high performance. Notably, we show that language models that have been finetuned on the same dataset form a tight cluster in the weight space, while models finetuned on different datasets from the same underlying task form a looser cluster. Moreover, traversing around the region between the models leads to new models that perform comparably or even better than models obtained via finetuning, even on tasks that the original models were not finetuned on. Our findings provide insight into the relationships between models, demonstrating that a model positioned between two similar models can acquire the knowledge of both. We leverage this and design a method for selecting a better model for efficient finetuning. Specifically, we show that starting from the center of the region is as effective, if not more, than using the pretrained model in 11 out of 12 datasets, resulting in an average accuracy improvement of 3.06.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep neural networks transfer layer-wise across different datasets and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks can be non-symmetric, is more influenced by dataset/task nature than architecture, and can quantify task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches in multi-task learning paradigms to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between two datasets or tasks can be non-symmetric.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to neural network architecture.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers.
Representations learned on more general datasets (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific datasets (e.g., SVHN).
papers.abstract: Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: On the Transferability of Representations in Neural Networks Between\n Datasets and Tasks
papers.research_question: How do representations in deep networks transfer between different datasets and tasks, and what factors influence this transferability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that layer-wise transferability of representations in deep networks is non-symmetric, influenced more by dataset nature than network architecture, and can serve as a proxy for task relatedness.
papers.conclusion: The observations highlight the importance of curriculum methods and structured approaches to designing systems for multiple tasks to maximize knowledge transfer and minimize interference between datasets or tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise transferability between datasets can be non-symmetric, e.g., features from CIFAR datasets are more transferable to SVHN than vice versa.
The nature of the datasets or tasks involved is more influential on transferability compared to the neural network architecture.
Initial layers in deep networks are more transferable than final layers across different tasks.
Layer-wise transferability can be used as a proxy for quantifying task relatedness.
Representations learned on more general classes (e.g., CIFAR) are more transferable than those learned on specific classes (e.g., SVHN digits).
papers.abstract:
Deep networks, composed of multiple layers of hierarchical distributed
representations, tend to learn low-level features in initial layers and
transition to high-level features towards final layers. Paradigms such as
transfer learning, multi-task learning, and continual learning leverage this
notion of generic hierarchical distributed representations to share knowledge
across datasets and tasks. Herein, we study the layer-wise transferability of
representations in deep networks across a few datasets and tasks and note some
interesting empirical observations.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Seeking Neural Nuggets: Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models from a Parametric Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether implicit knowledge stored in the parameters of a larger language model (teacher) can be transferred to a smaller model (student) through a parametric perspective.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parametric knowledge transfer paradigm that extracts task-specific parameters from a teacher model using sensitivity-based techniques and injects them into a student model via LoRA, demonstrating the transferability of implicit knowledge across LLMs of different scales.
papers.conclusion: Parametric knowledge transfer is feasible and effective; the proposed framework successfully transfers knowledge from larger to smaller LLMs, and the analysis highlights key factors that contribute to successful transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transferring extracted parameters from a teacher to a student model consistently improves the student's performance across reasoning, professional knowledge, instruction-driven, and open-ended conversation benchmarks.
The structural integrity of the extracted parameters (e.g., preserving submatrices) is crucial for effective transfer, outperforming random or single-weight extraction.
Sensitivity-based parameter extraction outperforms random selection, and the origin of parameters (which modules) matters more than the sheer number of parameters transferred.
Scaling up the teacher model generally leads to better student performance, even when there are architectural differences between models.
The number of seed samples used for sensitivity calculation and the initialization strategy for the LoRA module are important factors influencing transfer efficacy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently encode a wealth of knowledge within their parameters through pre-training on extensive corpora. While prior research has delved into operations on these parameters to manipulate the underlying implicit knowledge (encompassing detection, editing, and merging), there remains an ambiguous understanding regarding their transferability across models with varying scales. In this paper, we seek to empirically investigate knowledge transfer from larger to smaller models through a parametric perspective. To achieve this, we employ sensitivity-based techniques to extract and align knowledge-specific parameters between different LLMs. Moreover, the LoRA module is used as the intermediary mechanism for injecting the extracted knowledge into smaller models. Evaluations across four benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. Our findings highlight the critical factors contributing to the process of parametric knowledge transfer, underscoring the transferability of model parameters across LLMs of different scales. Project website: https://maszhongming.github.io/ParaKnowTransfer.

papers.title: Distillation Dynamics: Towards Understanding Feature-Based Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-based knowledge distillation, which works well for CNNs, fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), and what is the root cause of negative transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern (compression followed by expansion) and identifies a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models as the root cause of negative transfer in feature-based distillation, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViT compression strategies.
papers.conclusion: Successful knowledge transfer in Vision Transformers requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect the fundamental representational constraints and the U-shaped information processing dynamics of these architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models exhibit a learned U-shaped pattern in information entropy and activation magnitude across layers, indicating an initial compression phase followed by a task-specific expansion phase.
The failure of feature-based distillation in ViTs stems from a representational mismatch: teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity.
Late-layer feature alignment actively harms student performance (negative transfer) because it forces the student to adopt a representational paradigm incompatible with its capacity, disrupting its natural learning progression.
Frequency spectrum analysis shows teacher ViTs transition from low-pass to uniform, high-energy spectra in late layers, while CNNs maintain low-pass spectra, explaining why feature mimicry works for CNNs but fails for ViTs.
The U-shaped information processing signature is a consistent learned behavior across different ViT architectures (e.g., CaiT, standard ViT) and training paradigms (supervised, self-supervised like MAE).
papers.abstract: While feature-based knowledge distillation has proven highly effective for compressing CNNs, these techniques unexpectedly fail when applied to Vision Transformers (ViTs), often performing worse than simple logit-based distillation. We provide the first comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon through a novel analytical framework termed as "distillation dynamics", combining frequency spectrum analysis, information entropy metrics, and activation magnitude tracking. Our investigation reveals that ViTs exhibit a distinctive U-shaped information processing pattern: initial compression followed by expansion. We identify the root cause of negative transfer in feature distillation: a fundamental representational paradigm mismatch between teacher and student models. Through frequency-domain analysis, we show that teacher models employ distributed, high-dimensional encoding strategies in later layers that smaller student models cannot replicate due to limited channel capacity. This mismatch causes late-layer feature alignment to actively harm student performance. Our findings reveal that successful knowledge transfer in ViTs requires moving beyond naive feature mimicry to methods that respect these fundamental representational constraints, providing essential theoretical guidance for designing effective ViTs compression strategies. All source code and experimental logs are provided at https://github.com/thy960112/Distillation-Dynamics.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Teasing Apart Architecture and Initial Weights as Sources of Inductive Bias in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the inductive bias provided by a neural network's architecture be overridden by meta-learned initial weights, such that a given inductive bias can be realized equally well in different architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning can substantially reduce or eliminate performance differences across neural network architectures by learning appropriate initial weights, suggesting initial weights are a significant source of inductive bias that can override architectural biases in some settings, though architectural biases remain important for out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: While neural architectures impose constraints on what problems can be solved, these constraints are weak relative to the inductive biases afforded by initial weights; meta-learning can distill task-specific knowledge that reduces architectural differences, but architectural biases persist when generalization beyond the meta-training distribution is required.
papers.key_findings:
Meta-learning reduces or eliminates performance differences across architectures and data representations for in-distribution tasks.
Architectures that perform well without meta-learning also tend to meta-train more effectively.
All architectures generalize poorly on problems far from their meta-training experience, highlighting the need for stronger inductive biases for robust generalization.
In few-shot learning, CNNs are less sensitive to distribution shifts due to their spatial inductive biases.
LSTMs perform well on modular arithmetic tasks due to their sequential processing bias.
papers.limitation:
All architectures generalize poorly on problems that are far from their meta-training experience.
Meta-learning lacks the ability to distill stronger forms of generalization, such as extrapolation beyond the training task distribution.
future_direction: Exploring architectural constraints for stronger generalization
Using reinforcement learning to incentivize stronger generalization
Developing meta-learning variations that encourage finding structures beyond the data
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks can acquire many aspects of human knowledge from data, making them promising as models of human learning. But what those networks can learn depends upon their inductive biases -- the factors other than the data that influence the solutions they discover -- and the inductive biases of neural networks remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to draw conclusions about human learning from the performance of these systems. Cognitive scientists and machine learning researchers often focus on the architecture of a neural network as a source of inductive bias. In this paper we explore the impact of another source of inductive bias -- the initial weights of the network -- using meta-learning as a tool for finding initial weights that are adapted for specific problems. We evaluate four widely-used architectures -- MLPs, CNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers -- by meta-training 430 different models across three tasks requiring different biases and forms of generalization. We find that meta-learning can substantially reduce or entirely eliminate performance differences across architectures and data representations, suggesting that these factors may be less important as sources of inductive bias than is typically assumed. When differences are present, architectures and data representations that perform well without meta-learning tend to meta-train more effectively. Moreover, all architectures generalize poorly on problems that are far from their meta-training experience, underscoring the need for stronger inductive biases for robust generalization.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Understanding the Behaviors of BERT in Ranking
papers.research_question: What are the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks on MS MARCO and TREC Web Track?
papers.core_contribution: BERT is effective for QA-focused passage ranking due to its interaction-based seq2seq matching, but less effective for ad hoc document ranking where user click signals are more beneficial.
papers.conclusion: BERT excels in seq2seq matching tasks like MS MARCO due to its pre-training on surrounding contexts, but for ad hoc document ranking, pre-training on user clicks is more effective.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-based rankers outperform previous neural IR models on MS MARCO passage ranking.
BERT is not effective as a representation-based model for ranking; it relies on cross-sequence interactions.
On TREC ad hoc ranking, BERT underperforms compared to feature-based learning to rank and models pre-trained on user clicks.
BERT's attention focuses on marker tokens and stopwords, but stopwords have minimal impact on performance.
BERT assigns extreme ranking scores and depends on a few key terms, preferring semantic matches over loose relevance.
papers.limitation: BERT performs worse on TREC ad hoc ranking compared to models pre-trained on user clicks, indicating a gap between its pre-training on surrounding contexts and the needs of document ranking.
future_direction: Training deeper networks on user clicks signals
Studying deeper models trained on relevance-based labels compared to shallower neural rankers
papers.abstract: This paper studies the performances and behaviors of BERT in ranking tasks. We explore several different ways to leverage the pre-trained BERT and fine-tune it on two ranking tasks: MS MARCO passage reranking and TREC Web Track ad hoc document ranking. Experimental results on MS MARCO demonstrate the strong effectiveness of BERT in question-answering focused passage ranking tasks, as well as the fact that BERT is a strong interaction-based seq2seq matching model. Experimental results on TREC show the gaps between the BERT pre-trained on surrounding contexts and the needs of ad hoc document ranking. Analyses illustrate how BERT allocates its attentions between query-document tokens in its Transformer layers, how it prefers semantic matches between paraphrase tokens, and how that differs with the soft match patterns learned by a click-trained neural ranker.

papers.title: Optimal transfer protocol by incremental layer defrosting
papers.research_question: How to choose the optimal number of layers to freeze in transfer learning, and how does this optimal transfer depth depend on the amount of training data and the similarity between source and target tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a layer-wise defrosting protocol to identify the optimal transfer depth in transfer learning, showing that the optimal number of layers to freeze depends non-trivially on the target dataset size and source-target task similarity.
papers.conclusion: The layer-wise defrosting protocol can effectively identify the optimal transfer depth, which depends on data size and task similarity, and can significantly improve transfer learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The optimal transfer depth (number of layers to freeze) depends on the size of the target training set: with more data, it is better to defrost more layers.
The optimal transfer depth depends on the similarity between source and target tasks: more similar tasks allow transferring more layers.
Compliant learning: networks can achieve good accuracy even when early layers are constrained to be close to source weights, indicating degeneracy in parameter space.
Topological similarity of representations (measured by Information Imbalance) can predict transfer effectiveness.
The layer-wise defrosting protocol can yield significant performance gains over vanilla freezing, sometimes more than acquiring more data.
papers.limitation:
The approach lacks strong theoretical foundations.
No practical rule of thumb for identifying the best transfer protocol without explicit cross-validation on a target test set.
future_direction: Develop a training schedule for transfer learning capable of efficiently performing layer-wise defrosting in a fully automatic manner.
Understand how to disentangle input similarity from the labeling rule.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning is a powerful tool enabling model training with limited amounts of data. This technique is particularly useful in real-world problems where data availability is often a serious limitation. The simplest transfer learning protocol is based on ``freezing" the feature-extractor layers of a network pre-trained on a data-rich source task, and then adapting only the last layers to a data-poor target task. This workflow is based on the assumption that the feature maps of the pre-trained model are qualitatively similar to the ones that would have been learned with enough data on the target task. In this work, we show that this protocol is often sub-optimal, and the largest performance gain may be achieved when smaller portions of the pre-trained network are kept frozen. In particular, we make use of a controlled framework to identify the optimal transfer depth, which turns out to depend non-trivially on the amount of available training data and on the degree of source-target task correlation. We then characterize transfer optimality by analyzing the internal representations of two networks trained from scratch on the source and the target task through multiple established similarity measures.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: How transfer learning impacts linguistic knowledge in deep NLP models?
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impact the learned linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning redistributes linguistic knowledge in pre-trained language models, with BERT retaining it deeper in the network while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers, and the effect varies across downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning causes linguistic knowledge to be preserved in higher layers for some tasks and forgotten in others, with architectural differences: BERT retains knowledge deeper, while RoBERTa and XLNet localize it to lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
For some GLUE tasks (e.g., STS, RTE, MRPC), linguistic knowledge is preserved in higher layers after fine-tuning, while for others (e.g., SST, QNLI, MNLI) it is forgotten in higher layers.
BERT retains linguistic knowledge deeper in the network after fine-tuning, while RoBERTa and XLNet delegate it predominantly to lower layers.
Linguistic information becomes less distributed and less redundant in the network after fine-tuning, especially in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Salient linguistic neurons shift from higher to lower layers after fine-tuning in RoBERTa and XLNet.
Pruning bottom layers in RoBERTa and XLNet leads to more performance degradation than in BERT, consistent with the localization of linguistic knowledge to lower layers.
future_direction: Connecting linguistic probes with causation analysis on these tasks.
Detailed exploration of layer pruning patterns.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pre-trained neural language models towards downstream tasks has been a predominant theme in NLP recently. Several researchers have shown that deep NLP models learn non-trivial amount of linguistic knowledge, captured at different layers of the model. We investigate how fine-tuning towards downstream NLP tasks impacts the learned linguistic knowledge. We carry out a study across popular pre-trained models BERT, RoBERTa and XLNet using layer and neuronlevel diagnostic classifiers. We found that for some GLUE tasks, the network relies on the core linguistic information and preserve it deeper in the network, while for others it forgets. Linguistic information is distributed in the pre-trained language models but becomes localized to the lower layers post-fine-tuning, reserving higher layers for the task specific knowledge. The pattern varies across architectures, with BERT retaining linguistic information relatively deeper in the network compared to RoBERTa and XLNet, where it is predominantly delegated to the lower layers.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) structurally embed and acquire new knowledge during continual pre-training, from the perspective of knowledge circuit evolution?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the evolution of knowledge circuits during continual pre-training, revealing that new knowledge acquisition is influenced by relevance to existing knowledge, follows a biphasic (formation then optimization) pattern, and exhibits a deep-to-shallow component evolution.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the theoretical understanding of new knowledge acquisition mechanisms in LLMs and provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The acquisition of new knowledge is significantly influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge, with relevant new knowledge being integrated more efficiently than completely new knowledge.
The evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization, each marked by unique structural and behavioral characteristics.
The evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern, where mid-to-deeper layers first develop the extraction function, and later, lower layers enrich their knowledge representations.
The performance of knowledge circuits is positively correlated with knowledge frequency, with low-frequency knowledge circuits suffering from insufficient representations rather than fundamental capacity limitations.
The state of knowledge circuits could serve as a valuable tracking status for the continual pre-training process, enabling more informed adjustments to training.
future_direction: Utilizing data curriculums in continual pre-training to mimic the structure of the original corpus for more efficient integration.
Using the state of knowledge circuits as a tracking status to enable informed adjustments to training methods or data in response to different phases.
Further investigation into knowledge capacity scaling laws and their impact on model behavior during continual pre-training.
papers.abstract: Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern. These insights not only advance our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms of new knowledge acquisition in LLMs, but also provide potential implications for improving continual pre-training strategies to enhance model performance. Code and data will be available at https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in pretrained Transformers? Specifically, can we identify specific neurons responsible for expressing factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'knowledge neurons' and a gradient-based attribution method to identify neurons in feed-forward networks that express specific factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that factual knowledge in pretrained Transformers is stored in specific neurons within feed-forward networks, and these 'knowledge neurons' can be identified and manipulated to edit knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge neurons identified by the proposed method are positively correlated with the expression of their corresponding facts, as shown by suppression and amplification experiments.
Knowledge neurons are more activated by prompts that express the correct relation compared to prompts that do not.
Knowledge neurons for a fact are largely exclusive to that fact, with minimal overlap between facts of different relations.
Preliminary case studies show that directly modifying parameters associated with knowledge neurons can update or erase specific factual knowledge with moderate impact on other knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is based on the fill-in-the-blank cloze task, while knowledge can be expressed in more implicit ways.
The method uses single-word blanks in cloze queries, requiring extension to multi-word answers.
Interactions between knowledge neurons remain unexplored.
future_direction: Investigate whether Transformers can utilize stored knowledge in a generalized way, such as for reasoning.
Extend the method to multi-word blanks.
Explore how knowledge neurons work in multilingual pretrained Transformers.
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained language models are surprisingly good at recalling factual knowledge presented in the training corpus In this paper, we present preliminary studies on how factual knowledge is stored in pretrained Transformers by introducing the concept of knowledge neurons. Specifically, we examine the fill-in-the-blank cloze task for BERT. Given a relational fact, we propose a knowledge attribution method to identify the neurons that express the fact. We find that the activation of such knowledge neurons is positively correlated to the expression of their corresponding facts. In our case studies, we attempt to leverage knowledge neurons to edit (such as update, and erase) specific factual knowledge without fine-tuning. Our results shed light on understanding the storage of knowledge within pretrained Transformers. The code is available at https://github.com/ Hunter-DDM/knowledge-neurons.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: A Theory of How Pretraining Shapes Inductive Bias in Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How do weight initialization choices (absolute and relative scale across layers) impact the inductive bias and generalization error in the pretraining-fine-tuning pipeline?
papers.core_contribution: Develops an analytical theory of pretraining-fine-tuning in diagonal linear networks, showing how initialization parameters shape inductive bias and generalization, identifying four distinct fine-tuning regimes.
papers.conclusion: Initialization choices, especially the relative weight scales across layers, critically shape fine-tuning generalization by controlling the balance between reusing pretrained features and inducing continued feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
Different initialization choices lead to four distinct fine-tuning regimes: rich pretraining-independent, lazy pretraining-dependent, lazy pretraining-independent, and pretraining-dependent rich.
A smaller initialization scale in earlier layers enables both reuse and refinement of features, leading to superior generalization on fine-tuning tasks that rely on a subset of pretraining features.
The relative scale of initialization across layers plays a key role in entering the pretraining-dependent rich regime, which balances feature reuse and sparsity.
Pretraining and fine-tuning task parameters determine which of these regimes generalizes best.
Theoretical insights extend to nonlinear networks (ResNet-18) trained on CIFAR-100, showing similar effects of initialization on generalization.
papers.limitation: The theory is developed for diagonal linear networks, and its applicability to nonlinear networks with depth and other complexities may be limited.
future_direction: Extending the framework to nonlinear networks.
Measuring the ℓ-order and pretraining dependence in more complex architectures using influence functions.
papers.abstract: Pretraining and fine-tuning are central stages in modern machine learning systems. In practice, feature learning plays an important role across both stages: deep neural networks learn a broad range of useful features during pretraining and further refine those features during fine-tuning. However, an end-to-end theoretical understanding of how choices of initialization impact the ability to reuse and refine features during fine-tuning has remained elusive. Here we develop an analytical theory of the pretraining-fine-tuning pipeline in diagonal linear networks, deriving exact expressions for the generalization error as a function of initialization parameters and task statistics. We find that different initialization choices place the network into four distinct fine-tuning regimes that are distinguished by their ability to support feature learning and reuse, and therefore by the task statistics for which they are beneficial. In particular, a smaller initialization scale in earlier layers enables the network to both reuse and refine its features, leading to superior generalization on fine-tuning tasks that rely on a subset of pretraining features. We demonstrate empirically that the same initialization parameters impact generalization in nonlinear networks trained on CIFAR-100. Overall, our results demonstrate analytically how data and network initialization interact to shape fine-tuning generalization, highlighting an important role for the relative scale of initialization across different layers in enabling continued feature learning during fine-tuning.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: Analyzing the Effects of Supervised Fine-Tuning on Model Knowledge from Token and Parameter Levels
papers.research_question: How does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) affect a model's knowledge, and what are the mechanisms behind these effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that many parameter updates during SFT are unnecessary and can be restored to improve performance, providing guidance for better fine-tuning strategies.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that excessive parameter updates during SFT can harm model knowledge, and selectively restoring parameters can improve performance, guiding more effective fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Models fine-tuned on 1,920 samples can perform up to 14% worse than those fine-tuned on only 240 samples.
Performance fluctuates by over 12% depending on the knowledge mastery level of the fine-tuning data.
Up to 90% of parameter updates during SFT do not contribute to knowledge enhancement.
Restoring the most updated parameters to their pre-trained values can improve performance on CBQA tasks.
The KL divergence between fine-tuned and pre-trained models' token distributions initially decreases and then increases with more data, correlating with performance degradation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire substantial world knowledge during pre-training, which is further shaped by post-training techniques such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). However, the impact of SFT on a model's knowledge remains underexplored, limiting our ability to control knowledge change behavior in fine-tuned models. To address this gap, we evaluate closed-book question answering (CBQA) performance across five LLMs from the LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 families. Surprisingly, models fine-tuned on 1,920 samples perform up to 14% worse than those fine-tuned on only 240 samples. Furthermore, varying the level of knowledge mastery in the fine-tuning data leads to performance fluctuations of over 12%. To investigate these effects, we analyze model behavior at both the token and parameter levels. Our analysis reveals that up to 90% of parameter updates during SFT do not contribute to knowledge enhancement. Restoring these updates can improve performance on the CBQA task, depending on the characteristics of the fine-tuning data. These insights offer practical guidance for developing fine-tuning strategies that more effectively strengthen model knowledge.

papers.title: Understanding Learning Dynamics Through Structured Representations
papers.research_question: How do architectural structural choices influence learning dynamics, such as convergence, generalization, and adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structured neural architecture (PGNN) that decomposes layers into structured transformations and adaptive corrections, providing theoretical and empirical evidence that this design improves training stability, generalization, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The structured-corrective architecture (PGNN) provides a principled way to embed inductive biases into neural networks, improving stability and generalization while preserving flexibility, offering a new perspective on architectural design.
papers.key_findings:
Structured transformations improve gradient conditioning and reduce vanishing/exploding gradients.
PGNN exhibits smaller generalization gaps across layers, indicating more stable and generalizable internal representations.
The corrective path adaptively compensates for structural deficiencies, allowing a trade-off between structure and flexibility.
Theoretical analysis shows convergence guarantees under Lipschitz conditions for recursive dynamics.
Empirical results show improved robustness, faster convergence under alignment, and reduced sensitivity to initialization and gradient noise.
papers.abstract: While modern deep networks have demonstrated remarkable versatility, their training dynamics remain poorly understood--often driven more by empirical tweaks than architectural insight. This paper investigates how internal structural choices shape the behavior of learning systems. Building on prior efforts that introduced simple architectural constraints, we explore the broader implications of structure for convergence, generalization, and adaptation. Our approach centers on a family of enriched transformation layers that incorporate constrained pathways and adaptive corrections. We analyze how these structures influence gradient flow, spectral sensitivity, and fixed-point behavior--uncovering mechanisms that contribute to training stability and representational regularity. Theoretical analysis is paired with empirical studies on synthetic and structured tasks, demonstrating improved robustness, smoother optimization, and scalable depth behavior. Rather than prescribing fixed templates, we emphasize principles of tractable design that can steer learning behavior in interpretable ways. Our findings support a growing view that architectural design is not merely a matter of performance tuning, but a critical axis for shaping learning dynamics in scalable and trustworthy neural systems.

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: Layer-Wise Evolution of Representations in Fine-Tuned Transformers: Insights from Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the internal representations of transformers across different layers, and what is the progression from general to task-specific features?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning in transformers causes a structured progression of features across layers, where early layers retain general linguistic representations, middle layers act as transitional zones, and later layers become highly specialized for the task.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning transforms transformer representations in a layer-wise manner, with increasing task-specific specialization in deeper layers, providing insights into the adaptation process.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers (e.g., Layer 3) retain general linguistic representations but incorporate domain-specific features after fine-tuning.
Middle layers (e.g., Layer 6) encode a mix of general and task-specific features, shifting focus to structural tokens like punctuation after fine-tuning.
Late layers (e.g., Layer 12) become highly specialized for the task after fine-tuning, with clear differentiation based on task requirements such as sentiment polarity.
Cosine similarity analysis shows decreasing similarity between pre-trained and fine-tuned activations from early to late layers, indicating greater transformation in deeper layers.
Sparse AutoEncoders reveal that fine-tuning enhances task-specific feature encoding while preserving some general representations, demonstrating a layer-wise adaptation process.
future_direction: Expanding the scope to other transformer architectures and tasks, including multimodal and generative tasks.
Developing larger and more expressive Sparse AutoEncoders for better feature disentanglement.
Analyzing cases of poor task adaptation to understand failure modes in fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained transformers is a powerful technique for enhancing the performance of base models on specific tasks. From early applications in models like BERT to fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs), this approach has been instrumental in adapting general-purpose architectures for specialized downstream tasks. Understanding the fine-tuning process is crucial for uncovering how transformers adapt to specific objectives, retain general representations, and acquire task-specific features. This paper explores the underlying mechanisms of fine-tuning, specifically in the BERT transformer, by analyzing activation similarity, training Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs), and visualizing token-level activations across different layers. Based on experiments conducted across multiple datasets and BERT layers, we observe a steady progression in how features adapt to the task at hand: early layers primarily retain general representations, middle layers act as a transition between general and task-specific features, and later layers fully specialize in task adaptation. These findings provide key insights into the inner workings of fine-tuning and its impact on representation learning within transformer architectures.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
