papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How many memories can we add to a deep network by directly editing its weights? The paper investigates scaling up memory editing to thousands of associations in language models.
papers.core_contribution: MEMIT is a method for directly updating a language model with many memories by editing MLP weights in a range of critical layers, scaling to thousands of associations while maintaining generalization, specificity, and fluency.
papers.conclusion: MEMIT enables large-scale memory editing in transformers, and interpretability-based methods may become a practical alternative to opaque fine-tuning for editing, controlling, and auditing models.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT scales to 10,000 edits on GPT-J and GPT-NeoX, exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude.
MEMIT outperforms fine-tuning, MEND, and ROME baselines on efficacy, generalization, and specificity metrics.
MEMIT maintains fluency and consistency of generations after mass edits.
MEMIT performs well across different categories of facts and when editing mixed sets of memories.
Certain relations (e.g., 'plays sport') are harder to edit with robust specificity, but MEMIT still outperforms other methods.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to directional (subject, relation, object) associations and does not cover symmetric relations, spatial/temporal reasoning, mathematical knowledge, or procedural knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning Enhances Activation Intensity and Diversity in the Internal Circuitry of LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms by which RL fine-tuning enhances the capabilities of LLMs, and how do these mechanisms differ across RL algorithms like PPO, GRPO, and DPO?
papers.core_contribution: RL fine-tuning increases activation intensity and diversity in the internal circuitry of LLMs, with online RL (PPO, GRPO) showing consistent effects while DPO shows weaker or inconsistent changes.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs by increasing activation intensity and diversity, providing a mechanistic explanation for performance gains, with notable differences between online RL and preference-based methods like DPO.
papers.key_findings:
Online RL fine-tuning (PPO, GRPO) increases the average activation intensity of internal edges, engaging more pathways.
Online RL fine-tuning increases the diversity of activation patterns, as measured by higher entropy and lower kurtosis.
DPO fine-tuning does not consistently increase activation intensity or diversity, highlighting a methodological distinction from online RL.
The changes in internal circuitry are correlated with performance improvements in mathematical reasoning tasks.
The effects are consistent across multiple model families and mathematical datasets.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation is confined to mathematical reasoning tasks.
Memory overhead prevented analysis of models larger than 7B parameters.
The analyzed models are predominantly LLaMA-style architectures, limiting architectural diversity.
future_direction: Verify internal circuit dynamics in domains like code generation, creative writing, and open-ended dialogue.
Extend experiments to models larger than 7B parameters.
Explore a more diverse range of model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive prior knowledge through large-scale pretraining and can be further enhanced via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training. A growing body of evidence has shown that RL fine-tuning improves the capability of LLMs beyond what SFT alone achieves. However, the underlying mechanisms why RL fine-tuning is able to enhance the capability of various LLMs with distinct intrinsic characteristics remain underexplored. In this study, we draw inspiration from prior work on edge attribution patching (EAP) to investigate the internal differences of LLMs before and after RL fine-tuning. Our analysis across multiple model families and mathematical datasets shows two robust effects of online RL post-training: (i) an overall increase in average activation intensity, indicating that more internal pathways are engaged and their signals become stronger, and (ii) greater diversity in activation patterns, reflected by higher entropy and less concentrated edge distributions. These changes suggest that RL reshapes information flow to be both more redundant and more flexible, which may explain its advantage in mathematical generalization. Notably, models fine-tuned with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) deviate from these trends, exhibiting substantially weaker or inconsistent internal changes compared to PPO- and GRPO-based training. Together, our findings provide a unified view of how RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs and highlight the methodological distinctions between online RL and preference-based approaches. Our code is open source at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/llm_rl_probing_analysis.

papers.title: Empirical influence functions to understand the logic of fine-tuning
papers.research_question: How do individual training samples affect model outputs during fine-tuning, and do the resulting influence functions obey desirable properties such as semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces empirical influence functions (EIFs) to analyze fine-tuning, revealing that fine-tuning violates key desiderata for learning (e.g., logical consistency, causality), while prompting can partially rescue these failures.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuned models do not learn in a way that respects logical and causal relationships; prompting is a better way to incorporate new knowledge, suggesting models may be more like lookup machines than reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical influence functions show fine-tuning does not obey desiderata like decreasing influence with semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency.
For CNNs, the influence matrix is symmetric and noise has no influence on how much the model relies on a sample.
For LLMs (Phi-3), the influence matrix is asymmetric but does not reflect desired inferential asymmetry (e.g., transitivity, ontology, causality).
Prompting (in-context learning) can partially rescue these failures, leading to more asymmetric and logical influence functions.
Influence functions are densely populated, meaning models use irrelevant data as much as relevant data.
papers.limitation:
The approach is relatively slow, requiring fine-tuning for each training sample and then inference for each test sample.
The linearity assumption (neural tangent kernel) may not hold for all models.
The desiderata are superficial and not grounded in deep linguistic understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to the entire training process of LLMs.
Building meta-learning systems that optimize influence functions to obey the desiderata.
Using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a strategy to ameliorate the violations.
papers.abstract: Understanding the process of learning in neural networks is crucial for improving their performance and interpreting their behavior. This can be approximately understood by asking how a model's output is influenced when we fine-tune on a new training sample. There are desiderata for such influences, such as decreasing influence with semantic distance, sparseness, noise invariance, transitive causality, and logical consistency. Here we use the empirical influence measured using fine-tuning to demonstrate how individual training samples affect outputs. We show that these desiderata are violated for both for simple convolutional networks and for a modern LLM. We also illustrate how prompting can partially rescue this failure. Our paper presents an efficient and practical way of quantifying how well neural networks learn from fine-tuning stimuli. Our results suggest that popular models cannot generalize or perform logic in the way they appear to.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
papers.research_question: Can aligned behavior be transferred even when the teacher and student differ in architecture, task, and training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BIRD, a framework for transferring aligned behavior by distilling the structure of a teacher's internal representations into a student, without requiring shared data or tasks, and shows that transfer success is predictable by teacher representation properties.
papers.conclusion: BIRD provides a flexible, data-free mechanism for transferring aligned behavior across models and domains, advancing weak-to-strong generalization and enabling scalable, reusable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods in transferring out-of-distribution robustness, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the strongest baseline.
BIRD remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is 25× smaller than the student.
Three interpretable properties of the teacher’s representation space (task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success.
BIRD can improve weak-to-strong generalization in NLP when combined with soft-label distillation, though the effect is not universal.
Transfer success is predictable and actionable, offering practical guidance for teacher and layer selection.
papers.limitation:
Core analyses focus on robustness in vision, with only preliminary results in NLP.
Transfer success is likely bounded by the student’s capacity and task complexity.
Currently supervise alignment at a single layer; multi-layer or hierarchical extensions may be needed.
Effectiveness depends on the teacher; if the teacher encodes misaligned behaviors, BIRD may transfer them.
future_direction: Extending BIRD to other behaviors (e.g., honesty) and modalities (e.g., multimodal reasoning).
Quantifying the saturation effect of transfer success more precisely.
Exploring multi-layer or hierarchical extensions to capture deeper structural alignment.
papers.abstract: Human-aligned deep learning models exhibit behaviors consistent with human values, such as robustness, fairness, and honesty. Transferring these behavioral properties to models trained on different tasks or data distributions remains challenging: aligned behavior is easily forgotten during fine-tuning, and collecting task-specific data that preserves this behavior can be prohibitively costly. We introduce BIRD (Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation), a flexible framework for transferring aligned behavior by matching the internal representation structure of a student model to that of a teacher. Applied to out-of-distribution robustness in image classification, BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the next strongest baseline. It remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is $25 \times$ smaller than the student. In a large-scale study of over 400 teacher-student pairs, we show that three interpretable and computable properties of the teacher's representations (i.e., task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success. These insights offer practical guidance for teacher selection and design. BIRD turns small, well-aligned models into scalable alignment seeds, removing a key bottleneck in deploying safe AI systems in the wild.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity
papers.research_question: How does weight decay during language model pretraining affect model plasticity, i.e., the pretrained model’s ability to learn new knowledge during subsequent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that weight decay during pretraining improves model plasticity, leading to better downstream performance after fine-tuning, and that optimizing pretraining hyperparameters solely for validation loss may not yield the best downstream model.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay improves language model plasticity and downstream performance.
The optimal pretraining weight decay for downstream performance is larger than the default of 0.1.
Pretraining validation loss is not perfectly predictive of downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Weight decay encourages linearly separable representations in the model.
Weight decay reduces the rank of attention matrices and reduces overfitting on training data.
papers.limitation:
The benefits of increased plasticity must be weighed against other effects that may depend on model size, training duration, and other parameters of the training setup.
In heavily overtrained scenarios or for very large models, the benefits of lower pretraining validation loss may outweigh those of plasticity.
future_direction: Investigate trade-offs between stability and plasticity and the extent to which results hold in large-model and heavily overtrained scenarios.
Investigate the role of weight decay in model plasticity for foundation models beyond language (e.g., multimodal foundation models).
Investigate the role of weight decay for other downstream desiderata (e.g., safety alignment).
papers.abstract: The prevailing paradigm in large language model (LLM) development is to pretrain a base model, then perform further training to improve performance and model behavior. However, hyperparameter optimization and scaling laws have been studied primarily from the perspective of the base model's validation loss, ignoring downstream adaptability. In this work, we study pretraining from the perspective of model plasticity, that is, the ability of the base model to successfully adapt to downstream tasks through fine-tuning. We focus on the role of weight decay, a key regularization parameter during pretraining. Through systematic experiments, we show that models trained with larger weight decay values are more plastic, meaning they show larger performance gains when fine-tuned on downstream tasks. This phenomenon can lead to counterintuitive trade-offs where base models that perform worse after pretraining can perform better after fine-tuning. Further investigation of weight decay's mechanistic effects on model behavior reveals that it encourages linearly separable representations, regularizes attention matrices, and reduces overfitting on the training data. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role of that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.

papers.title: How Instruction and Reasoning Data shape Post-Training: Data Quality through the Lens of Layer-wise Gradients
papers.research_question: How do instruction and reasoning data of varying quality affect the layer-wise gradients during LLM post-training, and can existing data quality metrics be unified by spectral properties of these gradients?
papers.core_contribution: This work shows that various data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) can be unified by spectral properties of layer-wise gradients, specifically lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for higher-quality data, with effective rank being more robust. It also reveals that reasoning data induces higher effective ranks than instruction data.
papers.conclusion: Spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients provides a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, offering insights into training stability and data exploration strategies for post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Existing data quality metrics (IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, Reward) are unified by consistent spectral properties of gradients: lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks for high-quality data.
Effective rank outperforms nuclear norm in distinguishing low- vs. high-quality data and is more sensitive to subtle quality differences.
Reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, indicating richer gradient structures for complex tasks.
Within the same model family, layer-wise gradient spectral properties remain consistent across different model sizes, but diverge significantly across distinct model families.
Cosine similarities between gradients (same-layer and adjacent-layer) remain nearly zero and cannot reflect data quality.
papers.abstract: As the post-training of large language models (LLMs) advances from instruction-following to complex reasoning tasks, understanding how different data affect finetuning dynamics remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a spectral analysis of layer-wise gradients induced by low/high-quality instruction and reasoning data for LLM post-training. Our analysis reveals that widely-studied metrics for data evaluation, e.g., IFD, InsTag, Difficulty, and Reward, can be explained and unified by spectral properties computed from gradients' singular value decomposition (SVD). Specifically, higher-quality data are usually associated with lower nuclear norms and higher effective ranks. Notably, effective rank exhibits better robustness and resolution than nuclear norm in capturing subtle quality differences. For example, reasoning data achieves substantially higher effective ranks than instruction data, implying richer gradient structures on more complex tasks. Our experiments also highlight that models within the same family share similar gradient patterns regardless of their sizes, whereas different model families diverge significantly. Providing a unified view on the effects of data quality across instruction and reasoning data, this work illuminates the interplay between data quality and training stability, shedding novel insights into developing better data exploration strategies for post-training.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Where Multi-Task Learning Happens in Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent are different NLP tasks encoded in pre-trained LLMs? How does instruction tuning modify their representations, and do these effects generalize to unseen tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three functional groups of layers in instruction-tuned LLMs—shared, transition, and refinement layers—and shows how instruction tuning encodes task-specific information differently from pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The study maps layers in instruction-tuned LLMs to functional groups and demonstrates that instruction tuning enhances task-specific information encoding and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained LLMs already encode some tasks well, while others require instruction tuning.
Instruction tuning leads to the formation of shared layers (1-9), transition layers (10-15), and refinement layers (16-32) in Llama 2-SFT.
Instruction-tuned models show higher CKA similarities with task-specific control models in transition and refinement layers.
There is a positive correlation between task readability and CKA similarity in instruction-tuned models.
Instruction tuning improves generalization to unseen tasks by producing more general representations in lower layers.
papers.limitation:
Instruction tuning was implemented using LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, which may not capture all representational changes.
Computational constraints limited the exploration to the Llama 2 7B model and over 60 tasks.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained large language models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has become a common approach for building models that can solve various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, where and to what extent these models retain task-specific knowledge remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the task-specific information encoded in pre-trained LLMs and the effects of instruction tuning on their representations across a diverse set of over 60 NLP tasks. We use a set of matrix analysis tools to examine the differences between the way pre-trained and instruction-tuned LLMs store task-specific information. Our findings reveal that while some tasks are already encoded within the pre-trained LLMs, others greatly benefit from instruction tuning. Additionally, we pinpointed the layers in which the model transitions from high-level general representations to more task-oriented representations. This finding extends our understanding of the governing mechanisms of LLMs and facilitates future research in the fields of parameter-efficient transfer learning and multi-task learning.

papers.title: From Memorization to Reasoning in the Spectrum of Loss Curvature
papers.research_question: How are memorization and generalization represented and disentangled in transformer model weights using loss landscape curvature?
papers.core_contribution: Loss curvature (via K-FAC) disentangles memorization from generalization in transformer weights; editing low-curvature directions suppresses verbatim recitation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Loss curvature provides a unifying lens for separating memorization from generalization in Transformers, enabling effective recitation-reducing model editing and revealing a spectrum of model behaviors beyond strict memorization.
papers.key_findings:
K-FAC eigenvectors disentangle weight directions involved in memorized vs. non-memorized data, with low-curvature components activating more for memorization.
A weight-editing method that preserves high-curvature K-FAC components effectively suppresses untargeted memorization in LMs and ViTs, outperforming a supervised baseline (BalancedSubnet) on unseen data.
Tasks like arithmetic and closed-book fact retrieval rely more on low-curvature weight directions and are disproportionately harmed by edits, whereas logical reasoning is preserved or improved.
In ViTs, the editing method not only reduces memorization but can improve validation accuracy, acting as a regularizer.
The population-level curvature flattens for memorization directions, inverting the instance-level sharpness association, providing a unified view of memorization and generalization.
papers.limitation:
Makes no claims about fully removing memories, as methods may suffer from memorized data resurfacing after further tuning/perturbations.
The approximation of curvature (K-FAC) is not perfect, and estimating the bottommost eigenvalues could suffer from numerical stability issues.
future_direction: Explore whether models can be trained from the start to specialize for reasoning tasks, as results could possibly suggest.
Improve curvature approximations and fully explain why some tasks are more sensitive to perturbations.
papers.abstract: We characterize how memorization is represented in transformer models and show that it can be disentangled in the weights of both language models (LMs) and vision transformers (ViTs) using a decomposition based on the loss landscape curvature. This insight is based on prior theoretical and empirical work showing that the curvature for memorized training points is much sharper than non memorized, meaning ordering weight components from high to low curvature can reveal a distinction without explicit labels. This motivates a weight editing procedure that suppresses far more recitation of untargeted memorized data more effectively than a recent unlearning method (BalancedSubnet), while maintaining lower perplexity. Since the basis of curvature has a natural interpretation for shared structure in model weights, we analyze the editing procedure extensively on its effect on downstream tasks in LMs, and find that fact retrieval and arithmetic are specifically and consistently negatively affected, even though open book fact retrieval and general logical reasoning is conserved. We posit these tasks rely heavily on specialized directions in weight space rather than general purpose mechanisms, regardless of whether those individual datapoints are memorized. We support this by showing a correspondence between task data's activation strength with low curvature components that we edit out, and the drop in task performance after the edit. Our work enhances the understanding of memorization in neural networks with practical applications towards removing it, and provides evidence for idiosyncratic, narrowly-used structures involved in solving tasks like math and fact retrieval.

papers.title: Does Knowledge Localization Hold True? Surprising Differences Between Entity and Relation Perspectives in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether entity and relational knowledge are stored equivalently in language models and where relational knowledge is localized within model parameters.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that entity and relational knowledge are stored separately in language models, with relational knowledge encoded in both MLP and attention layers, challenging previous assumptions that knowledge is primarily localized in MLP weights.
papers.conclusion: This paper reveals that relational knowledge in LLMs is encoded not only in MLP layers but also significantly in attention modules, highlighting the complexity of knowledge storage mechanisms and providing a new foundation for future research in model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Editing entity knowledge does not equivalently edit relational knowledge, and vice versa, indicating they are not interchangeable.
Relational knowledge is localized in both MLP and attention layers, unlike entity knowledge which prior work suggested is primarily in MLP layers.
Knowledge storage location identified through causal tracing differs significantly between entity and relation perspectives.
Model editing from entity and relation perspectives yields inconsistent outcomes, questioning the validity of previous knowledge localization methods.
Factual knowledge is not stored as a single unit; relations and entities are represented separately within model parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models encapsulate knowledge and have demonstrated superior performance on various natural language processing tasks. Recent studies have localized this knowledge to specific model parameters, such as the MLP weights in intermediate layers. This study investigates the differences between entity and relational knowledge through knowledge editing. Our findings reveal that entity and relational knowledge cannot be directly transferred or mapped to each other. This result is unexpected, as logically, modifying the entity or the relation within the same knowledge triplet should yield equivalent outcomes. To further elucidate the differences between entity and relational knowledge, we employ causal analysis to investigate how relational knowledge is stored in pre-trained models. Contrary to prior research suggesting that knowledge is stored in MLP weights, our experiments demonstrate that relational knowledge is also significantly encoded in attention modules. This insight highlights the multifaceted nature of knowledge storage in language models, underscoring the complexity of manipulating specific types of knowledge within these models.

papers.title: Finding Experts in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: What is the presence of expert units in pre-trained Transformer Models, and how do they impact model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify expert units in transformer models, shows that the presence of these experts correlates with model generalization, and demonstrates how to use them for model evaluation and conditioned text generation without additional training.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that expert units are valuable for understanding, evaluating, and controlling transformer models, enabling applications like model ranking and concept-conditioned text generation.
papers.key_findings:
Expert units in transformer models are correlated with generalization power, with a squared Pearson correlation of 0.833.
Concepts with similar meanings share expert units, indicating co-learning, which can be used for explainability.
By forcing top expert units to be active, pre-trained language models can generate text containing specific concepts without fine-tuning.
Shallow layers in transformers acquire more concepts than deep layers, similar to observations in image GANs.
Homograph concepts are harder to disambiguate at the unit level compared to sense concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work we study the presence of expert units in pre-trained Transformer Models (TM), and how they impact a model's performance. We define expert units to be neurons that are able to classify a concept with a given average precision, where a concept is represented by a binary set of sentences containing the concept (or not). Leveraging the OneSec dataset (Scarlini et al., 2019), we compile a dataset of 1641 concepts that allows diverse expert units in TM to be discovered. We show that expert units are important in several ways: (1) The presence of expert units is correlated ($r^2=0.833$) with the generalization power of TM, which allows ranking TM without requiring fine-tuning on suites of downstream tasks. We further propose an empirical method to decide how accurate such experts should be to evaluate generalization. (2) The overlap of top experts between concepts provides a sensible way to quantify concept co-learning, which can be used for explainability of unknown concepts. (3) We show how to self-condition off-the-shelf pre-trained language models to generate text with a given concept by forcing the top experts to be active, without requiring re-training the model or using additional parameters.

papers.title: An Interpretable Neuron Embedding for Static Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide a sample- and class-independent explanation of neurons in a model, and can static knowledge from neuron semantics be used for knowledge distillation without sample-by-sample guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to embed neurons into semantic vectors for interpretability, enabling static knowledge distillation that performs comparably to existing methods without sample-by-sample teacher guidance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes neuron embedding for interpretability and static knowledge distillation, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer without instance-specific guidance.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic vectors accurately represent neuron semantics, as shown by similar activation maps for neurons with similar vectors.
The embedding method spontaneously converges to manually annotated semantic vectors without supervision.
Static knowledge distillation achieves performance comparable to or better than existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.
The method allows for analysis of neuron similar and additive relations.
Without sample-by-sample guidance, SKD is efficient and scalable.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have shown well-performance in various tasks, the poor interpretability of the models is always criticized. In the paper, we propose a new interpretable neural network method, by embedding neurons into the semantic space to extract their intrinsic global semantics. In contrast to previous methods that probe latent knowledge inside the model, the proposed semantic vector externalizes the latent knowledge to static knowledge, which is easy to exploit. Specifically, we assume that neurons with similar activation are of similar semantic information. Afterwards, semantic vectors are optimized by continuously aligning activation similarity and semantic vector similarity during the training of the neural network. The visualization of semantic vectors allows for a qualitative explanation of the neural network. Moreover, we assess the static knowledge quantitatively by knowledge distillation tasks. Empirical experiments of visualization show that semantic vectors describe neuron activation semantics well. Without the sample-by-sample guidance from the teacher model, static knowledge distillation exhibit comparable or even superior performance with existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer Memorization Recall Through Idioms
papers.research_question: When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodological framework and dataset for probing memorization recall in transformers, and finds that memorized predictions involve a two-step process of candidate promotion in early layers and confidence boosting in upper layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence.
Memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network.
The first layer is especially critical for memorized predictions.
The findings generalize from idioms to factual statements.
The IDIO MEM dataset is constructed for probing memorization and released for the community.
papers.abstract: To produce accurate predictions, language models (LMs) must balance between generalization and memorization. Yet, little is known about the mechanism by which transformer LMs employ their memorization capacity. When does a model decide to output a memorized phrase, and how is this phrase then retrieved from memory? In this work, we offer the first methodological framework for probing and characterizing recall of memorized sequences in transformer LMs. First, we lay out criteria for detecting model inputs that trigger memory recall, and propose idioms as inputs that typically fulfill these criteria. Next, we construct a dataset of English idioms and use it to compare model behavior on memorized vs. non-memorized inputs. Specifically, we analyze the internal prediction construction process by interpreting the model's hidden representations as a gradual refinement of the output probability distribution. We find that across different model sizes and architectures, memorized predictions are a two-step process: early layers promote the predicted token to the top of the output distribution, and upper layers increase model confidence. This suggests that memorized information is stored and retrieved in the early layers of the network. Last, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology beyond idioms in memorized factual statements. Overall, our work makes a first step towards understanding memory recall, and provides a methodological basis for future studies of transformer memorization.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Beyond Perplexity: A Lightweight Benchmark for Knowledge Retention in Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we measure factual knowledge retention during supervised fine-tuning, separate from stylistic learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KR-Test, a lightweight benchmark for evaluating factual knowledge retention during supervised fine-tuning, which separates factual learning from stylistic mimicry.
papers.conclusion: KR-Test provides a granular view of SFT dynamics by separating factual acquisition from stylistic alignment, enabling better monitoring and analysis of knowledge retention.
papers.key_findings:
KR-Test can distinguish factual learning from stylistic learning, unlike perplexity.
LoRA adapters placed on FFN layers achieve higher KR-Test scores than those on Attention layers under the same parameter budget.
Larger models (Llama-3.1-8B) show higher initial and final KR-Test scores compared to smaller models (Llama-3.2-1B), indicating scaling effects on factual retention.
Oracle validation shows that KR-Test questions are unambiguous (99.56% accuracy) and non-trivial for pre-trained models.
KR-Test provides a fine-grained signal for comparing PEFT design choices that are indistinguishable under perplexity.
papers.limitation:
KR-Test measures discriminative preference, not generative fidelity.
The analysis of parameter efficiency is limited to Llama-3.2-1B and may not be universal.
The robustness of KR-Test relies on the quality of automatically generated contrastive examples.
future_direction: Characterize the transfer function between discriminative preference and generative fidelity.
Establish correlation between KR-Test and downstream benchmarks (e.g., MMLU).
Investigate knowledge scaling laws.
papers.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is a standard approach for injecting domain knowledge into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, relying on validation perplexity to monitor training is often insufficient, as it confounds stylistic mimicry with genuine factual internalization. To address this, we introduce the Knowledge Retention (KR) Test , a lightweight, corpus-grounded evaluation framework designed to distinguish factual learning from linguistics. KR-Test utilizes automatically generated contrastive examples to measure likelihood preferences for correct versus incorrect continuations, requiring no instruction tuning or generative decoding. We validate the framework's integrity through a "blind vs. oracle" baseline analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the diagnostic capabilities of KR-Test by analyzing the training dynamics of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). By exposing the fine-grained dissociation between linguistic convergence and knowledge retention, KR-Test enhances the interpretability of fine-tuning dynamics.

papers.title: PMET: Precise Model Editing in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How can we achieve more precise model editing in transformers by optimizing the hidden states of individual components (MHSA and FFN) rather than the combined transformer layer hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PMET, a model editing method that optimizes hidden states of both MHSA and FFN but only updates FFN weights, based on the finding that MHSA acts as a knowledge extractor with general patterns.
papers.conclusion: We reveal that MHSA works as a knowledge extractor and encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns. Based on this finding, we propose PMET, which simultaneously optimizes the TC hidden states of both MHSA and FFN while only uses the optimized TC hidden states of FFN to perform precise updates of FFN weights. Our experiments on zsRE and COUNTERFACT demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of PMET.
papers.key_findings:
MHSA works as a knowledge extractor and encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns.
PMET achieves state-of-the-art performance on COUNTERFACT and zsRE datasets.
Simultaneously optimizing the TC hidden states of MHSA and FFN improves editing reliability compared to optimizing only FFN hidden states.
Updating MHSA weights slightly improves generalization but harms specificity.
Square root spread of residuals enhances reliability but leads to larger model changes, affecting specificity.
papers.limitation:
The partial opacity of LLMs’ internal mechanisms poses challenges for direct weight modification; edited models might not truly internalize knowledge and cannot reason using edited knowledge.
Benchmark and dataset construction have not strictly adhered to the subject-centric definition of model editing.
future_direction: Devise more sophisticated editing methods and evaluation metrics (e.g., MQuAKE, RIPPLEEDITS) to advance model editing.
papers.abstract: Model editing techniques modify a minor proportion of knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs) at a relatively low cost, which have demonstrated notable success. Existing methods assume Transformer Layer (TL) hidden states are values of key-value memories of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN). They usually optimize the TL hidden states to memorize target knowledge and use it to update the weights of the FFN in LLMs. However, the information flow of TL hidden states comes from three parts: Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA), FFN, and residual connections. Existing methods neglect the fact that the TL hidden states contains information not specifically required for FFN. Consequently, the performance of model editing decreases. To achieve more precise model editing, we analyze hidden states of MHSA and FFN, finding that MHSA encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns. This implies that MHSA weights do not require updating when new knowledge is introduced. Based on above findings, we introduce PMET, which simultaneously optimizes Transformer Component (TC, namely MHSA and FFN) hidden states, while only using the optimized TC hidden states of FFN to precisely update FFN weights. Our experiments demonstrate that PMET exhibits state-of-the-art performance on both the COUNTERFACT and zsRE datasets. Our ablation experiments substantiate the effectiveness of our enhancements, further reinforcing the finding that the MHSA encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns and indicating its storage of a small amount of factual knowledge. Our code is available at https://github.com/xpq-tech/PMET.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Cross-Task Linearity in the Pretraining-Finetuning Paradigm
papers.research_question: Does linear connectivity in feature space (Cross-Task Linearity) emerge between models finetuned on different tasks from a common pretrained checkpoint, and what insights does this provide for model merging/editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Cross-Task Linearity (CTL), where linearly interpolating weights of finetuned models leads to approximately linear interpolation of features, providing new insights into model averaging and task arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a linear connection between finetuned models, offering significant insights into model merging/editing techniques and advancing the understanding of pretraining and finetuning from a feature-centric perspective.
papers.key_findings:
CTL consistently occurs for finetuned models initialized from a common pretrained checkpoint across a wide range of settings.
Model averaging can be explained as the averaging of features at each layer, establishing a stronger connection between model averaging and logits ensemble.
Task arithmetic operations in parameter space (addition/negation of task vectors) correspond to linear operations in feature space, providing a feature-learning explanation.
Pretraining plays a crucial role in the emergence of CTL; without pretraining, CTL does not hold.
The emergence of CTL is associated with the flatness of the network landscape and the distance between the weights of two finetuned models.
papers.abstract: The pretraining-finetuning paradigm has become the prevailing trend in modern deep learning. In this work, we discover an intriguing linear phenomenon in models that are initialized from a common pretrained checkpoint and finetuned on different tasks, termed as Cross-Task Linearity (CTL). Specifically, we show that if we linearly interpolate the weights of two finetuned models, the features in the weight-interpolated model are often approximately equal to the linear interpolation of features in two finetuned models at each layer. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence supporting that CTL consistently occurs for finetuned models that start from the same pretrained checkpoint. We conjecture that in the pretraining-finetuning paradigm, neural networks approximately function as linear maps, mapping from the parameter space to the feature space. Based on this viewpoint, our study unveils novel insights into explaining model merging/editing, particularly by translating operations from the parameter space to the feature space. Furthermore, we delve deeper into the root cause for the emergence of CTL, highlighting the role of pretraining.

papers.title: Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does weight decay affect the update behavior of individual neurons in deep neural networks, and how does it lead to a steady state called rotational equilibrium that balances learning across layers and neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that weight decay induces rotational equilibrium, balancing angular updates across neurons, and that explicitly controlling rotation via Rotational Variants achieves the benefits of weight decay while reducing the need for learning rate warmup.
papers.conclusion: Weight decay induces rotational equilibrium and balanced rotation, which are key to the effectiveness of normalization and AdamW, and Rotational Variants can mimic this behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay causes the expected magnitude and angular updates of a neuron’s weight vector to converge to a steady state called rotational equilibrium.
Rotational equilibrium can be highly homogeneous, balancing the average rotation across different layers and neurons.
Explicitly controlling the angular updates via Rotational Optimizer Variants provides the benefits of weight decay while reducing the need for learning rate warmup.
Balanced rotation contributes to the performance benefit of AdamW over Adam with ℓ2-regularization and of Weight Standardization.
The interaction of weight decay and learning rate shapes the rotation in the initial transient phase and results in two distinct effective step sizes in steady state.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how weight decay affects the update behavior of individual neurons in deep neural networks through a combination of applied analysis and experimentation. Weight decay can cause the expected magnitude and angular updates of a neuron's weight vector to converge to a steady state we call rotational equilibrium. These states can be highly homogeneous, effectively balancing the average rotation -- a proxy for the effective learning rate -- across different layers and neurons. Our work analyzes these dynamics across optimizers like Adam, Lion, and SGD with momentum, offering a new simple perspective on training that elucidates the efficacy of widely used but poorly understood methods in deep learning. We demonstrate how balanced rotation plays a key role in the effectiveness of normalization like Weight Standardization, as well as that of AdamW over Adam with L2-regularization. Finally, we show that explicitly controlling the rotation provides the benefits of weight decay while substantially reducing the need for learning rate warmup.

papers.title: Pretraining with Artificial Language: Studying Transferable Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining with an artificial language that has a nesting dependency structure provides transferable knowledge to natural language tasks, and the transferred knowledge is related to position-aware context dependence.
papers.conclusion: The transferable knowledge in pretrained encoders can be characterized as position-aware context dependence, meaning tokens in a sequence can be characterized by their neighbor tokens at specific positions.
papers.key_findings:
Pretraining with an artificial language that models statistical dependency within a sentence (Log-linear) provides a useful inductive bias for natural language modeling.
A nesting head-to-tail dependency structure is more beneficial for transfer than a flat structure.
Encoders pretrained on languages with nesting dependency structures are better at capturing local contextual information, which is important for tasks like dependency parsing.
The amount of contextual information encoded by the pretrained encoder (as measured by a probing task) correlates with its transfer performance in some cases.
The Uniform and Zipf languages, which lack token dependencies, degrade encoder performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation: The knowledge of position-aware context dependence may not explain every aspect of the success of cross-lingual transfer.
future_direction: Investigate how model size affects the transferability of the encoder.
Investigate if there is any difference in the knowledge transferred among different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate what kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language. We design artificial languages with structural properties that mimic natural language, pretrain encoders on the data, and see how much performance the encoder exhibits on downstream tasks in natural language. Our experimental results show that pretraining with an artificial language with a nesting dependency structure provides some knowledge transferable to natural language. A follow-up probing analysis indicates that its success in the transfer is related to the amount of encoded contextual information and what is transferred is the knowledge of position-aware context dependence of language. Our results provide insights into how neural network encoders process human languages and the source of cross-lingual transferability of recent multilingual language models.

papers.title: IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is used to specialize model behavior by training weights to produce intended target responses for queries. In contrast, In-Context Learning (ICL) adapts models during inference with instructions or demonstrations in the prompt. ICL can offer better generalizability and more calibrated responses compared to SFT in data scarce settings, at the cost of more inference compute. In this work, we ask the question: Can ICL's internal computations be used to improve the qualities of SFT? We first show that ICL and SFT produce distinct activation patterns, indicating that the two methods achieve adaptation through different functional mechanisms. Motivated by this observation and to use ICL's rich functionality, we introduce ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation technique which aims to replicate ICL's activation patterns in SFT models and incentivizes ICL-like internal reasoning. Performing IA2 as a priming step before SFT significantly improves the accuracy and calibration of model outputs, as shown by our extensive empirical results on 12 popular benchmarks and two model families. This finding is not only practically useful, but also offers a conceptual window into the inner mechanics of model adaptation.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Localized Definitions and Distributed Reasoning: A Proof-of-Concept Mechanistic Interpretability Study via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How is knowledge representation localized in fine-tuned language models, and how does it vary with task complexity?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that factual knowledge is localized while associative knowledge is distributed in fine-tuned models, and introduces CLAP for causal layer attribution.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is localized while associative reasoning depends on distributed intermediate representations, highlighting task-dependent knowledge organization.
papers.key_findings:
Patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference for associative knowledge, indicating distributed representations.
Patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery) for definitional knowledge, indicating localized representation.
Minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01).
Editing efficacy depends on task type, with factual knowledge more localized and associative knowledge depending on distributed representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis focused exclusively on PubMed epilepsy-related abstracts, potentially limiting generalizability to broader knowledge tasks.
Activation patching may generate false positives due to indirect causal pathways.
Exclusive focus on GPT-2 leaves open questions about scalability to other architectures.
future_direction: Cross-domain comparisons to better understand task-dependent representation patterns.
Methodological integration to improve efficiency.
Extensions to multimodal models where knowledge distribution mechanisms may differ significantly.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the localization of knowledge representation in fine-tuned GPT-2 models using Causal Layer Attribution via Activation Patching (CLAP), a method that identifies critical neural layers responsible for correct answer generation. The model was fine-tuned on 9,958 PubMed abstracts (epilepsy: 20,595 mentions, EEG: 11,674 mentions, seizure: 13,921 mentions) using two configurations with validation loss monitoring for early stopping. CLAP involved (1) caching clean (correct answer) and corrupted (incorrect answer) activations, (2) computing logit difference to quantify model preference, and (3) patching corrupted activations with clean ones to assess recovery. Results revealed three findings: First, patching the first feedforward layer recovered 56% of correct preference, demonstrating that associative knowledge is distributed across multiple layers. Second, patching the final output layer completely restored accuracy (100% recovery), indicating that definitional knowledge is localised. The stronger clean logit difference for definitional questions further supports this localized representation. Third, minimal recovery from convolutional layer patching (13.6%) suggests low-level features contribute marginally to high-level reasoning.
