Statistical analysis confirmed significant layer-specific effects (p<0.01). These findings demonstrate that factual knowledge is more localized and associative knowledge depends on distributed representations. We also showed that editing efficacy depends on task type. Our findings not only reconcile conflicting observations about localization in model editing but also emphasize on using task-adaptive techniques for reliable, interpretable updates.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Joint learning of interpretation and distillation
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input, and proposes methods to explain the distilled model and use explanation imitation to improve distillation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel explanation solution for the GBDT2NN distilled model by using interpretation vectors from the teacher model, and introduces a joint learning method that uses explanation as an auxiliary task to improve prediction performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that imitating the explanation of the teacher model is an effective means to improve the performance of distillation models and provides interpretability for the distilled model.
papers.key_findings:
The independent interpretable method can generate explanations for GBDT2NN that are highly correlated with the teacher model's explanations, as measured by NDCG and top-k coverage.
The joint method, which incorporates interpretation learning into the distillation process, improves the prediction performance of GBDT2NN on several benchmarks.
The joint method also leads to faster convergence during training compared to the standard GBDT2NN model.
Visual evaluation on MNIST datasets shows the proposed method can accurately identify important features (pixels) for classification.
papers.abstract: The extra trust brought by the model interpretation has made it an indispensable part of machine learning systems. But to explain a distilled model's prediction, one may either work with the student model itself, or turn to its teacher model. This leads to a more fundamental question: if a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input? This question becomes even more crucial when the two models have dramatically different structure, taking GBDT2NN for example. This paper conducts an empirical study on the new approach to explaining each prediction of GBDT2NN, and how imitating the explanation can further improve the distillation process as an auxiliary learning task. Experiments on several benchmarks show that the proposed methods achieve better performance on both explanations and predictions.

papers.title: Anatomy of Catastrophic Forgetting: Hidden Representations and Task Semantics
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting affect the hidden representations of neural networks, and how is it influenced by task semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that catastrophic forgetting is primarily driven by changes in deeper layers, and that forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in higher layers, mitigation methods stabilize these layers, and forgetting is maximized for tasks of intermediate similarity, providing a foundation for understanding and mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper layers are the primary source of forgetting in neural networks.
Forgetting mitigation methods like elastic weight consolidation and replay buffers act by stabilizing deeper layer representations.
Forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
Representational similarity (measured by CKA) between tasks is key to understanding forgetting.
A novel CIFAR-100 distribution shift task approximates realistic input distribution shift for studying forgetting.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in developing versatile machine learning systems is catastrophic forgetting: a model trained on tasks in sequence will suffer significant performance drops on earlier tasks. Despite the ubiquity of catastrophic forgetting, there is limited understanding of the underlying process and its causes. In this paper, we address this important knowledge gap, investigating how forgetting affects representations in neural network models. Through representational analysis techniques, we find that deeper layers are disproportionately the source of forgetting. Supporting this, a study of methods to mitigate forgetting illustrates that they act to stabilize deeper layers. These insights enable the development of an analytic argument and empirical picture relating the degree of forgetting to representational similarity between tasks. Consistent with this picture, we observe maximal forgetting occurs for task sequences with intermediate similarity. We perform empirical studies on the standard split CIFAR-10 setup and also introduce a novel CIFAR-100 based task approximating realistic input distribution shift.

papers.title: BitFit: Simple Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning for Transformer-based Masked Language-models
papers.research_question: Can fine-tuning only the bias terms of a pre-trained transformer model achieve competitive performance compared to full fine-tuning, and what does this imply about the nature of the fine-tuning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BitFit, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that updates only the bias terms of transformer models, achieving competitive performance with full fine-tuning, especially for small-to-medium data, and supporting the hypothesis that fine-tuning exposes pre-existing knowledge rather than learning new task-specific knowledge.
papers.conclusion: BitFit is an effective, parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that modifies only bias terms, easing deployment and raising questions about the role of bias terms and fine-tuning dynamics in pre-trained transformers.
papers.key_findings:
BitFit, which fine-tunes only the bias terms (0.08-0.09% of parameters), achieves performance competitive with full fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark.
For small-to-medium training data, BitFit sometimes outperforms full fine-tuning, as shown on SQuAD subsets.
Fine-tuning only a subset of bias terms (query and middle-of-MLP biases) still yields competitive results, using only 0.04% of parameters.
Randomly selecting the same number of parameters to fine-tune performs substantially worse, indicating bias terms are special for adaptation.
BitFit models exhibit a smaller generalization gap (difference between training and test error) compared to fully fine-tuned models.
future_direction: Further analysis of the role of bias terms in pre-trained networks
Investigation of fine-tuning dynamics in transformers
papers.abstract: We introduce BitFit, a sparse-finetuning method where only the bias-terms of the model (or a subset of them) are being modified. We show that with small-to-medium training data, applying BitFit on pre-trained BERT models is competitive with (and sometimes better than) fine-tuning the entire model. For larger data, the method is competitive with other sparse fine-tuning methods. Besides their practical utility, these findings are relevant for the question of understanding the commonly-used process of finetuning: they support the hypothesis that finetuning is mainly about exposing knowledge induced by language-modeling training, rather than learning new task-specific linguistic knowledge.

papers.title: Cross-Model Semantics in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do structural constraints affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures? To what extent are learned representations tied to specific architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes representational alignment across architectures and demonstrates that structural regularities induce more stable representational geometry, improving interoperability of learned features.
papers.conclusion: PGNN integrates structural priors to enhance learning efficiency and generalization, and structural constraints can improve representational transferability across models.
papers.key_findings:
PGNN exhibits faster convergence and slightly higher test accuracy compared to baseline MLP.
Ablation shows that removing structural projection in PGNN leads to lower performance, confirming its utility.
PGNN shows similar robustness to initialization noise as MLP, with slight advantages under mild noise.
Representational alignment metrics show that structured representations can be partially aligned across architectures.
The framework enables measurement of alignment using CKA, subspace overlap, and transfer accuracy.
papers.limitation: Extrapolation to more complex datasets like CIFAR-10 did not show a major advantage for PGNN.
future_direction: Adapting and scaling PGNN to broader domains and more complex data distributions.
papers.abstract: The internal representations learned by deep networks are often sensitive to architecture-specific choices, raising questions about the stability, alignment, and transferability of learned structure across models. In this paper, we investigate how structural constraints--such as linear shaping operators and corrective paths--affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures. Building on the insights from prior studies on structured transformations and convergence, we develop a framework for measuring and analyzing representational alignment across networks with distinct but related architectural priors. Through a combination of theoretical insights, empirical probes, and controlled transfer experiments, we demonstrate that structural regularities induce representational geometry that is more stable under architectural variation. This suggests that certain forms of inductive bias not only support generalization within a model, but also improve the interoperability of learned features across models. We conclude with a discussion on the implications of representational transferability for model distillation, modular learning, and the principled design of robust learning systems.

papers.title: Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether performance drops in continual learning are due to a loss of underlying knowledge or a decline in task alignment.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of 'spurious forgetting' in continual learning, attributing performance drops to a loss of task alignment rather than knowledge, and proposes a Freeze strategy (freezing bottom layers) to mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the critical distinction between task alignment and knowledge retention in continual learning, and the Freeze strategy provides an effective way to maintain alignment and reduce forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Performance drops in continual learning are often due to a decline in task alignment, not the loss of underlying knowledge.
Early optimization steps on a new task can rapidly undo the alignment established for previous tasks.
Analyzing weight updates shows orthogonal directions between tasks, particularly in bottom layers, explaining the alignment shift.
Freezing the bottom layers of the model during continual learning effectively mitigates spurious forgetting and improves performance across multiple scenarios.
The proposed Freeze strategy outperforms other continual learning techniques like regularization and replay methods in sequential fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
A notable limitation is the persistent accuracy gap compared to data replay methods, which retain more old data.
There is a trade-off between stability and plasticity; freezing too many layers may hinder adaptation to new tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) reveal a perplexing phenomenon in continual learning: despite extensive training, models experience significant performance declines, raising questions about task alignment and underlying knowledge retention. This study first explores the concept of "spurious forgetting", proposing that such performance drops often reflect a decline in task alignment rather than true knowledge loss. Through controlled experiments with a synthesized dataset, we investigate the dynamics of model performance during the initial training phases of new tasks, discovering that early optimization steps can disrupt previously established task alignments. Our theoretical analysis connects these shifts to orthogonal updates in model weights, providing a robust framework for understanding this behavior. Ultimately, we introduce a Freezing strategy that fix the bottom layers of the model, leading to substantial improvements in four continual learning scenarios. Our findings underscore the critical distinction between task alignment and knowledge retention, paving the way for more effective strategies in continual learning.

papers.title: Exact learning dynamics of deep linear networks with prior knowledge
papers.research_question: How does prior knowledge embedded in initial network weights affect learning dynamics in deep linear networks?
papers.core_contribution: Derives exact solutions for the gradient flow dynamics of deep linear networks with prior knowledge, revealing how initializations affect learning trajectories and internal representations.
papers.conclusion: The results provide a mathematical toolkit for understanding the impact of prior knowledge on deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Explicit solutions for the network function, internal representational similarity, and neural tangent kernel over training for a broad class of initializations and tasks.
Identifies a class of task-independent initializations that lead to fast exponential learning dynamics while converging to rich internal representations.
Analyzes how network weights dynamically align with task structure during learning.
Provides exact solutions for continual learning, reversal learning, and learning of structured representations.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to deep linear networks, which are simpler than nonlinear networks.
papers.abstract: Learning in deep neural networks is known to depend critically on the knowledge embedded in the initial network weights. However, few theoretical results have precisely linked prior knowledge to learning dynamics. Here we derive exact solutions to the dynamics of learning with rich prior knowledge in deep linear networks by generalising Fukumizu’s matrix Riccati solution (Fukumizu 1998 Gen 1 1E-03). We obtain explicit expressions for the evolving network function, hidden representational similarity, and neural tangent kernel over training for a broad class of initialisations and tasks. The expressions reveal a class of task-independent initialisations that radically alter learning dynamics from slow non-linear dynamics to fast exponential trajectories while converging to a global optimum with identical representational similarity, dissociating learning trajectories from the structure of initial internal representations. We characterise how network weights dynamically align with task structure, rigorously justifying why previous solutions successfully described learning from small initial weights without incorporating their fine-scale structure. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for continual learning, reversal learning and learning of structured knowledge. Taken together, our results provide a mathematical toolkit for understanding the impact of prior knowledge on deep learning.

papers.title: Knowledge is Not Enough: Injecting RL Skills for Continual Adaptation
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently adapt LLMs to new knowledge with reasoning skills, without performing expensive Reinforcement Learning (RL) in the target domain?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Parametric Skill Transfer (PaST), a framework that extracts a domain-agnostic skill vector from a source domain trained with RL and linearly injects it into a target model after lightweight SFT, enabling efficient knowledge adaptation without target-domain RL.
papers.conclusion: PaST effectively transfers reasoning and execution skills to models adapted to new knowledge, enabling efficient and robust adaptation without the need for expensive reinforcement learning in the target domain.
papers.key_findings:
Parameter updates induced by SFT (knowledge) and RL (skills) are nearly orthogonal, indicating they occupy disentangled subspaces.
The extracted skill vector can be transferred to a target domain, significantly improving performance on knowledge-intensive QA and agentic tool-use tasks without performing RL in the target domain.
PaST outperforms strong SFT baselines and the state-of-the-art self-editing method SEAL on SQuAD, and shows strong scalability to long-context QA (LooGLE) and cross-domain generalization in tool use (ToolBench).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face the "knowledge cutoff" challenge, where their frozen parametric memory prevents direct internalization of new information. While Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is commonly used to update model knowledge, it often updates factual content without reliably improving the model's ability to use the newly incorporated information for question answering or decision-making. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is essential for acquiring reasoning skills; however, its high computational cost makes it impractical for efficient online adaptation. We empirically observe that the parameter updates induced by SFT and RL are nearly orthogonal. Based on this observation, we propose Parametric Skill Transfer (PaST), a framework that supports modular skill transfer for efficient and effective knowledge adaptation. By extracting a domain-agnostic Skill Vector from a source domain, we can linearly inject knowledge manipulation skills into a target model after it has undergone lightweight SFT on new data. Experiments on knowledge-incorporation QA (SQuAD, LooGLE) and agentic tool-use benchmarks (ToolBench) demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. On SQuAD, PaST outperforms the state-of-the-art self-editing SFT baseline by up to 9.9 points. PaST further scales to long-context QA on LooGLE with an 8.0-point absolute accuracy gain, and improves zero-shot ToolBench success rates by +10.3 points on average with consistent gains across tool categories, indicating strong scalability and cross-domain transferability of the Skill Vector.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Beyond Neural Incompatibility: Easing Cross-Scale Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models through Latent Semantic Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we enable effective and efficient knowledge transfer across LLMs of different scales? The paper investigates using activations as the medium and latent semantic alignment as a prerequisite for parametric knowledge transfer.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a semantics-first method for parametric knowledge transfer that uses layer outputs as the medium and aligns latent semantics between teacher and student models, enabling stable cross-scale transfer.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating activations as the carrier of knowledge and aligning semantics-first provides a robust path to cross-scale parametric knowledge transfer, as demonstrated by SemAlign.
papers.key_findings:
SemAlign improves student performance over task-matched baselines and parameter-space transfer baselines on four benchmarks.
Performing latent semantic alignment before any parameter update strongly predicts stable cross-scale transfer.
Steering a small set of paired layers is enough to induce broader behavioral alignment, making the method efficient.
SemAlign extracts and transfers teacher competency more reliably, especially when the teacher is stronger in coding.
The method avoids neural incompatibility by using activations as the carrier of knowledge and aligning semantics first.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a limited set of tasks and layer-level pairing; broader coverage (architectures, modalities, safety-critical settings) remains open.
future_direction: Extending semantic alignment to finer granularity (sub-layer, attention head).
Comparing objectives that combine causal and semantic constraints.
Exploring better strategies on layer pairing based on layer outputs.
Scaling analyses across families with larger architectural gaps to stress-test robustness.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode vast amounts of knowledge in their massive parameters, which is accessible to locate, trace, and analyze. Despite advances in neural interpretability, it is still not clear how to transfer knowledge in a fine-grained manner, namely parametric knowledge transfer (PKT). A key problem is enabling effective and efficient knowledge transfer across LLMs of different scales, which is essential for achieving greater flexibility and broader applicability in transferring knowledge between LLMs. Due to neural incompatibility, referring to the architectural and parametric differences between LLMs of varying scales, existing methods that directly reuse layer parameters are severely limited. In this paper, we identify the semantic alignment in latent space as the fundamental prerequisite for LLM cross-scale knowledge transfer. Instead of directly using the layer parameters, our approach takes activations as the medium of layer-wise knowledge transfer. Leveraging the semantics in latent space, our approach is simple and outperforms prior work, better aligning model behaviors across varying scales. Evaluations on four benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our method. Further analysis reveals the key factors easing cross-scale knowledge transfer and provides insights into the nature of latent semantic alignment.

papers.title: Concept Distillation: Leveraging Human-Centered Explanations for Model Improvement
papers.research_question: If CAVs can identify and quantify sensitivity to concepts, can they also be used to improve the model? Can we learn less biased and more human-centered models?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc model improvement via a concept loss and concept distillation using a teacher model, enabling model debiasing and prior knowledge induction.
papers.conclusion: Concept distillation and concept loss provide a framework for improving model interpretability, reducing biases, and inducing prior knowledge by leveraging human-centered explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-sensitive training with a concept loss can debias models on synthetic (ColorMNIST, DecoyMNIST, TextureMNIST) and real-world (BFFHQ) datasets.
Using a large pre-trained teacher model (DINO) for concept distillation improves concept learning and debiasing performance compared to using the student model alone.
Extending CAV sensitivity calculation to intermediate layers via class prototypes enhances the method's effectiveness.
The method can induce human-centered concepts as priors in non-classification tasks, demonstrated on Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID).
The approach is zero-shot and does not require architectural changes or direct concept supervision.
papers.abstract: Humans use abstract concepts for understanding instead of hard features. Recent interpretability research has focused on human-centered concept explanations of neural networks. Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) estimate a model's sensitivity and possible biases to a given concept. In this paper, we extend CAVs from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc training in order to reduce model bias through fine-tuning using an additional Concept Loss. Concepts were defined on the final layer of the network in the past. We generalize it to intermediate layers using class prototypes. This facilitates class learning in the last convolution layer, which is known to be most informative. We also introduce Concept Distillation to create richer concepts using a pre-trained knowledgeable model as the teacher. Our method can sensitize or desensitize a model towards concepts. We show applications of concept-sensitive training to debias several classification problems. We also use concepts to induce prior knowledge into IID, a reconstruction problem. Concept-sensitive training can improve model interpretability, reduce biases, and induce prior knowledge. Please visit https://avani17101.github.io/Concept-Distilllation/ for code and more details.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does fine-tuning underperform linear probing out-of-distribution, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and underperform linear probing out-of-distribution when pretrained features are good and distribution shift is large; linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT) combines the benefits of both methods.
papers.conclusion: LP-FT is a simple, effective method for robust fine-tuning that mitigates the tradeoff between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning achieves higher in-distribution accuracy but lower out-of-distribution accuracy than linear probing on large distribution shifts.
Theoretical analysis shows fine-tuning distorts pretrained features because the feature extractor changes more for in-distribution examples than out-of-distribution examples.
Linear probing preserves pretrained features and extrapolates better out-of-distribution but cannot adapt features to the downstream task.
LP-FT (linear probing then fine-tuning) outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
Feature distortion in fine-tuning is due to random head initialization; initializing with a linear probed head reduces distortion.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis is limited to linear models and may not capture all aspects of deep neural networks.
future_direction: Extend theoretical analysis to non-linear models and neural tangent kernel regime.
Develop even better methods for robust fine-tuning inspired by the analysis.
papers.abstract: When transferring a pretrained model to a downstream task, two popular methods are full fine-tuning (updating all the model parameters) and linear probing (updating only the last linear layer -- the "head"). It is well known that fine-tuning leads to better accuracy in-distribution (ID). However, in this paper, we find that fine-tuning can achieve worse accuracy than linear probing out-of-distribution (OOD) when the pretrained features are good and the distribution shift is large. On 10 distribution shift datasets (Breeds-Living17, Breeds-Entity30, DomainNet, CIFAR $\to$ STL, CIFAR10.1, FMoW, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-Sketch), fine-tuning obtains on average 2% higher accuracy ID but 7% lower accuracy OOD than linear probing. We show theoretically that this tradeoff between ID and OOD accuracy arises even in a simple setting: fine-tuning overparameterized two-layer linear networks. We prove that the OOD error of fine-tuning is high when we initialize with a fixed or random head -- this is because while fine-tuning learns the head, the lower layers of the neural network change simultaneously and distort the pretrained features. Our analysis suggests that the easy two-step strategy of linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT), sometimes used as a fine-tuning heuristic, combines the benefits of both fine-tuning and linear probing. Empirically, LP-FT outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing on the above datasets (1% better ID, 10% better OOD than full fine-tuning).

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: A Closer Look at How Fine-tuning Changes BERT
papers.research_question: Does fine-tuning always improve performance? How does fine-tuning alter the representation to adjust for downstream tasks? How does fine-tuning change the geometric structure of different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning adjusts representations to downstream tasks by grouping same-label points and pushing label clusters apart, which improves performance, and does so while largely preserving the original spatial structure of the data points.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning adjusts representations to downstream tasks by altering the geometry of the embedding space—simplifying non-linear structures and increasing inter-cluster distances—while largely preserving the original spatial structure, which explains its widespread effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning does not always improve performance; an exception was found where it hurt performance, correlated with high divergence between training and test sets.
For representations where task labels are not linearly separable, fine-tuning simplifies the space by grouping points with the same label into fewer clusters.
For linearly separable representations, fine-tuning increases the distances between clusters of different labels, enlarging the separation region and improving generalization.
Fine-tuning introduces a divergence between training and test sets, but this is usually not severe enough to hurt generalization.
Fine-tuning does not arbitrarily change higher layers; they remain similar to the original representation, preserving the relative positions of label clusters.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the BERT family of models for English tasks; findings may not generalize to other languages or model architectures.
The analysis ignores the structure within each cluster, which is another source of information about the representation.
future_direction: Investigating how the divergence between training and test sets affects generalization and whether it represents a new kind of overfitting.
Developing theoretical analysis to connect geometric findings (e.g., inter-cluster distances) to representation learnability.
Analyzing model parameters during fine-tuning to understand why higher layers change more than lower layers.
Extending the analysis to other languages and model architectures.
Investigating the structure within clusters for further insights.
papers.abstract: Given the prevalence of pre-trained contextualized representations in today's NLP, there have been many efforts to understand what information they contain, and why they seem to be universally successful. The most common approach to use these representations involves fine-tuning them for an end task. Yet, how fine-tuning changes the underlying embedding space is less studied. In this work, we study the English BERT family and use two probing techniques to analyze how fine-tuning changes the space. We hypothesize that fine-tuning affects classification performance by increasing the distances between examples associated with different labels. We confirm this hypothesis with carefully designed experiments on five different NLP tasks. Via these experiments, we also discover an exception to the prevailing wisdom that "fine-tuning always improves performance". Finally, by comparing the representations before and after fine-tuning, we discover that fine-tuning does not introduce arbitrary changes to representations; instead, it adjusts the representations to downstream tasks while largely preserving the original spatial structure of the data points.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
papers.research_question: How do large language models acquire, retain, and forget concepts during continual pretraining? Specifically, how do internal concept representations correlate with concept acquisition and forgetting, and how do they relate to interference and synergy among multiple concepts and knowledge types during joint training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a circuit-level analysis of concept learning in LLMs during continual pre-training, revealing that concept circuits provide signals for learning and forgetting dynamics, and show patterns like stage-wise temporal changes and interference/synergy effects.
papers.conclusion: The work offers a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and informs the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting.
Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization.
Concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training.
Semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones.
Conceptual knowledge differs in transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others.
papers.limitation:
Limited model scale, focusing only on GPT-2 Large and LLaMA-3.2-1B, not larger models.
Exploration of actionable training strategies is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending analysis to larger-scale models.
Exploring circuit-aware training effort allocation and interference-aware data scheduling.
papers.abstract: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal Concept Circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate Graph Metrics to characterize circuit structure. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization; (3) concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training; (4) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (5) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings offer a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and inform the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.

papers.title: Learning to Interpret Weight Differences in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we make finetuning-induced weight changes ('weight diffs') in language models interpretable? The paper investigates training models to describe their own finetuning-induced modifications using natural language.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Diff Interpretation Tuning (DIT), a method that trains a low-rank adapter to enable finetuned language models to generate accurate natural language descriptions of the behavioral changes encoded in their finetuning-induced weight modifications.
papers.conclusion: DIT is a promising approach for interpreting weight diffs via introspection, but scaling up the method with larger and more diverse training data is essential for improving generalization and making it applicable to real-world weight diffs.
papers.key_findings:
DIT successfully describes weight diffs in two proof-of-concept settings: reporting hidden behaviors (e.g., backdoors) and summarizing finetuned knowledge.
DIT adapters trained on rank-1 LoRA weight diffs generalize to accurately describing higher rank LoRA diffs and show non-trivial generalization to full-parameter finetuning.
DIT adapters generalize to out-of-distribution triggers (e.g., zero-width spaces) not seen during training.
DIT adapters show essentially no cross-behavior generalization (e.g., an adapter trained for hidden topics fails on news summarization and vice versa).
DIT struggles to uncover the triggers of hidden behaviors, succeeding in 0 out of 100 test samples for trigger inversion.
papers.limitation:
DIT adapters have limited generalization across different behaviors (e.g., a topic adapter does not work for news summarization).
DIT fails to uncover the triggers of hidden behaviors, suggesting trigger inversion may be inherently harder than behavior discovery.
The current method's generalization is limited by the small size and lack of diversity of the training data.
future_direction: Scaling up DIT with larger and more diverse training sets of weight diffs, questions, and answers.
Improving architectures for DIT, e.g., to allow lossless access to model internals with and without the weight diff applied.
Enabling models to perform extended introspective 'reasoning' to solve harder introspection tasks, potentially requiring RL-based training schemes.
papers.abstract: Finetuning (pretrained) language models is a standard approach for updating their internal parametric knowledge and specializing them to new tasks and domains. However, the corresponding model weight changes ("weight diffs") are not generally interpretable. While inspecting the finetuning dataset can give a sense of how the model might have changed, these datasets are often not publicly available or are too large to work with directly. Towards the goal of comprehensively understanding weight diffs in natural language, we introduce Diff Interpretation Tuning (DIT), a method that trains models to describe their own finetuning-induced modifications. Our approach uses synthetic, labeled weight diffs to train a DIT-adapter, which can be applied to a compatible finetuned model to make it describe how it has changed. We demonstrate in two proof-of-concept settings (reporting hidden behaviors and summarizing finetuned knowledge) that our method enables models to describe their finetuning-induced modifications using accurate natural language descriptions.

papers.title: Fine-tuning can cripple your foundation model; preserving features may be the solution
papers.research_question: How does end-to-end fine-tuning of a foundation model affect its pre-trained knowledge, and can we reduce the resulting concept forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new fine-tuning regularizer (LDIFS) that minimizes the ℓ2 distance in feature space between the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, significantly reducing concept forgetting while maintaining downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: Concept forgetting is a significant undesirable side effect of fine-tuning foundation models, and the proposed LDIFS method provides an effective solution by preserving pre-trained features during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
End-to-end fine-tuning of foundation models causes significant 'concept forgetting', where the model loses its ability to recognize concepts outside the downstream task.
Regularizing the fine-tuned model to stay close to the pre-trained model in parameter space (L2SP) helps reduce concept forgetting, but regularizing in feature space is more effective.
The proposed LDIFS method, which preserves features from multiple internal representations, outperforms existing fine-tuning methods in minimizing concept forgetting without harming downstream task accuracy.
LDIFS is also effective in a continual fine-tuning setup, outperforming both standard fine-tuning and classic continual learning baselines in preserving and accumulating knowledge across a sequence of tasks.
Preserving only the last-layer features is not effective; preserving features from different internal representations is crucial for reducing concept forgetting.
papers.limitation:
LDIFS has a hyperparameter λ that requires cross-validation, and the cross-validated value may not always yield the best model for concept forgetting or downstream performance.
The paper uses a fixed set of evenly spaced features; an analysis of which features are useful for encoding which concepts is an open question.
If the pre-trained model contains biases and undesirable behaviors, LDIFS may preserve them in the fine-tuned model.
The study is limited to CLIP and image classification tasks; understanding concept forgetting in other foundation model families (e.g., LLMs) is left for future work.
future_direction: Investigating better ways to set the LDIFS hyperparameter λ.
Analyzing which features are useful for encoding which concepts.
Studying how to prevent undesirable behaviors (e.g., biases) from being distilled into the fine-tuned model while preserving pre-trained knowledge.
Extending the study of concept forgetting to other foundation model families such as Large Language Models.
Fundamentally defining what a 'concept' is and the granularity at which we should study it for foundation models.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained foundation models, due to their enormous capacity and exposure to vast amounts of data during pre-training, are known to have learned plenty of real-world concepts. An important step in making these pre-trained models effective on downstream tasks is to fine-tune them on related datasets. While various fine-tuning methods have been devised and have been shown to be highly effective, we observe that a fine-tuned model's ability to recognize concepts on tasks $\textit{different}$ from the downstream one is reduced significantly compared to its pre-trained counterpart. This is an undesirable effect of fine-tuning as a substantial amount of resources was used to learn these pre-trained concepts in the first place. We call this phenomenon ''concept forgetting'' and via experiments show that most end-to-end fine-tuning approaches suffer heavily from this side effect. To this end, we propose a simple fix to this problem by designing a new fine-tuning method called $\textit{LDIFS}$ (short for $\ell_2$ distance in feature space) that, while learning new concepts related to the downstream task, allows a model to preserve its pre-trained knowledge as well. Through extensive experiments on 10 fine-tuning tasks we show that $\textit{LDIFS}$ significantly reduces concept forgetting. Additionally, we show that LDIFS is highly effective in performing continual fine-tuning on a sequence of tasks as well, in comparison with both fine-tuning as well as continual learning baselines.

papers.title: Fine-Tuned Transformers Show Clusters of Similar Representations Across Layers
papers.research_question: How do learned representations change after fine-tuning pretrained language encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuned RoBERTa and ALBERT models exhibit a block diagonal structure in layer representation similarity, and later layers can be discarded without hurting performance.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuned RoBERTa and ALBERT models show a consistent pattern of representation similarity with two distinct layer clusters, and later layers can be discarded. ELECTRA models differ, prompting further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuned RoBERTa and ALBERT show a block diagonal structure in representation similarity across layers, with strong similarity within early and late layer clusters.
Later layers of fine-tuned RoBERTa and ALBERT can be discarded without performance loss, even without further tuning.
ELECTRA models do not exhibit the same block diagonal structure and are less tolerant to layer truncation.
Skipping the first layer heavily impacts performance, while skipping later layers has minimal impact.
Later layer representations in fine-tuned models are highly dissimilar to those in the base pretrained model.
papers.limitation: The findings may not generalize to all pretrained models, as ELECTRA shows different behavior.
future_direction: Investigate why ELECTRA models exhibit different representation similarity patterns compared to RoBERTa and ALBERT.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of fine-tuning pretrained language encoders like BERT for downstream natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, it is still poorly understood how neural networks change after fine-tuning. In this work, we use centered kernel alignment (CKA), a method for comparing learned representations, to measure the similarity of representations in task-tuned models across layers. In experiments across twelve NLU tasks, we discover a consistent block diagonal structure in the similarity of representations within fine-tuned RoBERTa and ALBERT models, with strong similarity within clusters of earlier and later layers, but not between them. The similarity of later layer representations implies that later layers only marginally contribute to task performance, and we verify in experiments that the top few layers of fine-tuned Transformers can be discarded without hurting performance, even with no further tuning.

papers.title: Forgetting before Learning: Utilizing Parametric Arithmetic for Knowledge Updating in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can knowledge updating in large language models be made more effective by first forgetting old knowledge to avoid conflict with new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes F-Learning, a two-stage fine-tuning paradigm that uses parametric arithmetic to forget old knowledge before learning new knowledge, improving knowledge updating performance in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: F-Learning is an effective paradigm for knowledge updating that mitigates conflict between old and new knowledge, and forgetting via LoRA can be as effective as via full fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
F-Learning improves knowledge updating performance over direct fine-tuning and outperforms existing baselines in most cases.
Forgetting old knowledge by subtracting LoRA parameters can achieve a similar effect to subtracting full fine-tuning parameters, with lower computational cost.
The forgetting operation is effective, as model performance on old knowledge decreases with increasing forgetting rate.
Parameter analysis shows that full fine-tuning forgetting leads to significant changes in MLP layers, while LoRA forgetting only affects attention layers.
F-Learning has minimal impact on other model capabilities such as mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension.
papers.limitation:
Adds extra computation due to an extra forgetting process.
More relevant theoretical foundations need to be researched, such as the existence form of specific knowledge.
future_direction: Generalize the proposed method from single-modal domain to multi-modal domains of knowledge.

papers.title: How a student becomes a teacher: learning and forgetting through Spectral methods
papers.research_question: Can an invariant subnetwork be identified in an overparameterized student network that mimics a teacher network, and can a spectral optimization method achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: A spectral training method that, with regularization, identifies an invariant subnetwork within an overparameterized student network that mirrors the teacher's structure and retains full performance when pruned.
papers.conclusion: The spectral training method enables identification of a minimal, efficient subnetwork that retains performance and recovers the teacher's topological features, outperforming conventional weight decay and parametrization.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral method with regularization identifies an invariant subnetwork in the student that matches the teacher's size.
Pruning based on eigenvalue magnitude does not degrade performance until the invariant core is removed, exhibiting a phase-transition-like behavior.
The path distribution of the pruned student matches that of the teacher, unlike conventionally trained networks.
The method generalizes to various datasets (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR-100) and architectures (e.g., ResNet50).
The spectral parametrization yields a node importance ranking via eigenvalues, enabling effective structural pruning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments employ straightforward student network architectures; more complex architectures need to be tested for general conclusions.
The method has been validated on relatively simple datasets; generalization to more complex, real-world datasets is an open question.
The analysis focuses on ranking nodes in hidden layers; input neurons are not included, which could provide insights on relevant features.
future_direction: Extending the parametrization techniques to more advanced network architectures.
Testing the proposed techniques on larger and more complex real-world datasets.
Including input neurons in the analysis to identify key relevant features.
papers.abstract: In theoretical ML, the teacher-student paradigm is often employed as an effective metaphor for real-life tuition. The above scheme proves particularly relevant when the student network is overparameterized as compared to the teacher network. Under these operating conditions, it is tempting to speculate that the student ability to handle the given task could be eventually stored in a sub-portion of the whole network. This latter should be to some extent reminiscent of the frozen teacher structure, according to suitable metrics, while being approximately invariant across different architectures of the student candidate network. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art conventional learning techniques could not help in identifying the existence of such an invariant subnetwork, due to the inherent degree of non-convexity that characterizes the examined problem. In this work, we take a leap forward by proposing a radically different optimization scheme which builds on a spectral representation of the linear transfer of information between layers. The gradient is hence calculated with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors with negligible increase in terms of computational and complexity load, as compared to standard training algorithms. Working in this framework, we could isolate a stable student substructure, that mirrors the true complexity of the teacher in terms of computing neurons, path distribution and topological attributes. When pruning unimportant nodes of the trained student, as follows a ranking that reflects the optimized eigenvalues, no degradation in the recorded performance is seen above a threshold that corresponds to the effective teacher size. The observed behavior can be pictured as a genuine second-order phase transition that bears universality traits.

papers.title: When Data Falls Short: Grokking Below the Critical Threshold
papers.research_question: Can knowledge distillation from a grokked model induce and accelerate grokking on a different data distribution, and can grokking occur when training data falls below the critical threshold?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge Distillation (KD) from a grokked model can induce and accelerate grokking on a different data distribution, even when the available data is below the critical threshold, and does not require weight decay or decreasing weight norms.
papers.conclusion: KD enables grokking below the critical data threshold and across varying distributions, offering a practical solution for efficient training under data scarcity and distribution shift.
papers.key_findings:
KD from a grokked teacher model enables a student model to grok on a different distribution, even when the student's training data is below the critical size.
Grokking can occur without weight decay and with increasing weight norms, challenging prior theories that link grokking to weight norm reduction.
In joint training on two distributions, standard supervised training fails when either distribution has insufficient data, but KD from grokked models enables generalization.
In a continual pretraining setup, KD mitigates catastrophic forgetting when a model transitions from one distribution to another.
KD provides a stronger learning signal than ground-truth labels in low-data regimes, enabling grokking where standard training fails.
future_direction: Extend these insights to more complex tasks.
Deepen our understanding of grokking’s mechanisms.
Explore broader uses of pre-grokked models that generalize reliably and adapt efficiently to dynamic real-world data.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of grokking, where models exhibit delayed generalization following overfitting on training data. We focus on data-scarce regimes where the number of training samples falls below the critical threshold, making grokking unobservable, and on practical scenarios involving distribution shift. We first show that Knowledge Distillation (KD) from a model that has already grokked on a distribution (p1) can induce and accelerate grokking on a different distribution (p2), even when the available data lies below the critical threshold. This highlights the value of KD for deployed models that must adapt to new distributions under limited data. We then study training on the joint distribution (p1, p2) and demonstrate that while standard supervised training fails when either distribution has insufficient data, distilling from models grokked on the individual distributions enables generalization. Finally, we examine a continual pretraining setup, where a grokked model transitions from p1 to p2, and find that KD both accelerates generalization and mitigates catastrophic forgetting, achieving strong performance even with only 10% of the data. Together, our results provide new insights into the mechanics of grokking under knowledge transfer and underscore the central role of KD in enabling generalization in low-data and evolving distribution settings.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
papers.research_question: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theory and algorithms based on neuron activation subspace match to analyze representation similarity in neural networks, and finds that representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as expected.
papers.conclusion: Representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as prevalently expected, raising fundamental questions about learning representations and interpretability in deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Maximum match similarity is low for most convolutional layers, indicating low overall similarity of representations.
Layers close to input and output show higher similarity due to alignment with input data and output targets, respectively.
Simple matches are rarely of small size, indicating that single neurons or small neuron clusters do not learn similar representations.
The structure of matches can be characterized by maximum matches and simple matches, which can be found efficiently with the proposed algorithms.
The findings raise questions about whether networks learn completely different representations or if subspace match is not the right metric for similarity.
papers.limitation: Subspace match may not be the right metric for measuring the similarity of representations.
papers.abstract: It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive, there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations. Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

papers.title: Learning to Remember from a Multi-Task Teacher
papers.research_question: How can we reduce catastrophic forgetting at the representation level in sequential learning, and can a meta-learning algorithm that mimics a multi-task teacher's representation achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a measure of catastrophic forgetting at the representation level using a linear readout layer and introduces a meta-learning algorithm that learns weight updates to mimic a multi-task teacher's representation, thereby reducing representational forgetting in sequential learning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed meta-learner can overcome catastrophic forgetting while improving performance on new tasks and generalizes to unseen classes, initializations, and domains, though scaling to longer sequences remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed meta-learner significantly reduces representational forgetting on old tasks while maintaining good performance on new tasks.
The meta-learner generalizes to unseen classes, unseen network initialization checkpoints, and unseen data domains (e.g., from CIFAR to Tiny-ImageNet).
The meta-learner can handle sequential learning with more than two tasks, though performance on intermediate tasks is not as strong as on the first task.
The meta-learner's output (gradient multiplier) is non-trivial and can sometimes be negative, indicating it learns to dynamically modify gradient directions to prevent forgetting.
Representational forgetting, measured by a linear readout layer, shows a significant drop in performance on old tasks even when the output layer is re-learned, indicating that forgetting occurs at the representation level.
papers.limitation: The meta-learner currently generalizes well up to 600 steps but finds it challenging to generalize to even longer sequences.
future_direction: Training the meta-learner with longer sequences and more sequential tasks with more computational resources.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning typically focus on fixing the accuracy of the predictions for a previously learned task. In this paper we argue that the outputs of neural networks are subject to rapid changes when learning a new data distribution, and networks that appear to "forget" everything still contain useful representation towards previous tasks. Instead of enforcing the output accuracy to stay the same, we propose to reduce the effect of catastrophic forgetting on the representation level, as the output layer can be quickly recovered later with a small number of examples. Towards this goal, we propose an experimental setup that measures the amount of representational forgetting, and develop a novel meta-learning algorithm to overcome this issue. The proposed meta-learner produces weight updates of a sequential learning network, mimicking a multi-task teacher network's representation. We show that our meta-learner can improve its learned representations on new tasks, while maintaining a good representation for old tasks.

papers.title: Neuronal Fluctuations: Learning Rates vs Participating Neurons
papers.research_question: How does the learning rate affect the magnitude and character of weight and bias fluctuations in neural networks, and how does this relate to model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that learning rate affects neuron engagement and reconstruction quality in autoencoders, with higher learning rates leading to better reconstruction but more inactive neurons, while lower learning rates engage more neurons but require longer training.
papers.conclusion: The learning rate significantly influences neural fluctuations and neuron participation, impacting model performance and highlighting the exploration-exploitation trade-off in training.
papers.key_findings:
Learning rate of 0.01 yields the best reconstruction but has the highest number of inactive neurons.
Learning rate of 0.001 provides comparable reconstruction with similar inactive neurons as 0.01.
Learning rate of 0.0001 results in the poorest reconstruction but engages the majority of neurons in learning.
Approximately 50 neurons remained inactive throughout the 1000-epoch training across learning rates.
Fluctuations in weights, biases, activations, and gradients vary with learning rate, affecting learning dynamics.
papers.limitation: Training was limited to 1000 epochs, which may not be sufficient for lower learning rates to achieve optimal reconstruction.
future_direction: Investigating the effect on accuracy by pruning inactive neurons.
Analyzing the layer-wise impact of different learning rates.
Studying the effect on power and resource consumption during training and inference.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) rely on inherent fluctuations in their internal parameters (weights and biases) to effectively navigate the complex optimization landscape and achieve robust performance. While these fluctuations are recognized as crucial for escaping local minima and improving generalization, their precise relationship with fundamental hyperparameters remains underexplored. A significant knowledge gap exists concerning how the learning rate, a critical parameter governing the training process, directly influences the dynamics of these neural fluctuations. This study systematically investigates the impact of varying learning rates on the magnitude and character of weight and bias fluctuations within a neural network. We trained a model using distinct learning rates and analyzed the corresponding parameter fluctuations in conjunction with the network's final accuracy. Our findings aim to establish a clear link between the learning rate's value, the resulting fluctuation patterns, and overall model performance. By doing so, we provide deeper insights into the optimization process, shedding light on how the learning rate mediates the crucial exploration-exploitation trade-off during training. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of hyperparameter tuning and the underlying mechanics of deep learning.

papers.title: Unveiling Knowledge Utilization Mechanisms in LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge stream within the RAG framework, and how do LLM modules function in knowledge utilization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unveils the intrinsic knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLMs in RAG scenarios from macroscopic (knowledge streaming) and microscopic (module functions) perspectives, introducing KAPE to identify knowledge-specific neurons and demonstrating how deactivating them can shift the model's reliance between internal and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how LLMs integrate internal and external knowledge in RAG, advancing interpretability and paving the way for designing more efficient and controllable LLM architectures capable of balancing parametric and contextual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge streaming within RAG can be divided into four distinct stages: knowledge refinement, elicitation, expression, and contestation.
The relevance of retrieved passages guides the knowledge streaming, primarily affecting the knowledge elicitation stage.
The proposed KAPE metric can identify neurons associated with internal or external knowledge, and selectively deactivating these neurons can alter the LLM's preference for one knowledge source over the other.
Multi-head attention (MHA) and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules have complementary roles: MHA facilitates information integration, while MLP layers help verify knowledge accuracy and are sensitive to factual correctness.
The LLM evaluates the relevance between the query and external knowledge during the knowledge elicitation stage via information flow between them.
future_direction: Future work will focus on refining these mechanisms to improve real-world applications and extend the boundaries of AI-driven knowledge retrieval systems, developing more nuanced models that better handle the complexities of knowledge integration.
papers.abstract: Considering the inherent limitations of parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely employed to expand their knowledge scope. Since RAG has shown promise in knowledge-intensive tasks like open-domain question answering, its broader application to complex tasks and intelligent assistants has further advanced its utility. Despite this progress, the underlying knowledge utilization mechanisms of LLM-based RAG remain underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation of the intrinsic mechanisms by which LLMs integrate internal (parametric) and external (retrieved) knowledge in RAG scenarios. Specially, we employ knowledge stream analysis at the macroscopic level, and investigate the function of individual modules at the microscopic level. Drawing on knowledge streaming analyses, we decompose the knowledge utilization process into four distinct stages within LLM layers: knowledge refinement, knowledge elicitation, knowledge expression, and knowledge contestation. We further demonstrate that the relevance of passages guides the streaming of knowledge through these stages. At the module level, we introduce a new method, knowledge activation probability entropy (KAPE) for neuron identification associated with either internal or external knowledge. By selectively deactivating these neurons, we achieve targeted shifts in the LLM's reliance on one knowledge source over the other. Moreover, we discern complementary roles for multi-head attention and multi-layer perceptron layers during knowledge formation. These insights offer a foundation for improving interpretability and reliability in retrieval-augmented LLMs, paving the way for more robust and transparent generative solutions in knowledge-intensive domains.
